activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Adolphe Thiers's History of the French Revolution, published from 1823 to 1827, praised moderate leaders such as Mirabeau and Lafayette and condemned radicals such as Robespierre.
story:
The public library smelled of carpet cleaner and old glue, and Landon had claimed the corner table by the window because it was the only one with an outlet and a view of anything other than shelving. Ms. Rossi had assigned the essay on Friday: how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, a historiographical essay, which meant he was not supposed to write about the Revolution at all. He was supposed to write about the writing. He had read the assignment sheet four times over the weekend and understood it less each time.

He spread his sources like a card player. Three library books, two printouts, his notebook open to a page that said only "thesis??" in increasingly angry handwriting. The whole project enervated him; he could feel it draining the energy out of his Saturday the way a crack drained a bathtub. He had wanted to do the easy thing, the movie version: poor risen people, corrupt king, guillotine, done. But the assignment kept pulling him sideways, asking not what happened but who told it and when and what they were afraid of.

Gwendolyn dropped into the chair across from him with a smoothie and no apology. "Still on the French thing?"

"It's not a French thing. It's a French thing about French things." He turned his laptop toward her. "Look. This guy Adolphe Thiers wrote a History of the French Revolution, published from 1823 to 1827. It was huge, everybody read it. And in it he praises the moderates, Mirabeau, Lafayette, and condemns the radicals. He calls Robespierre basically a fanatic."

"So?"

"So Thiers wrote history before he ran France. He ended up leading the government decades later. Doesn't that bother you? He picked his heroes and his villains in print, and then he got power."

Gwendolyn stirred her smoothie, which had separated into layers nobody would call appetizing. "Maybe he picked them because he believed it. People are allowed to believe things before they get power."

"That's the problem. I can't tell the difference between belief and positioning, and the assignment says I have to have a considered position on which historians got it right, or at least how the getting-it changed." He rubbed his eyes. "There's this other book, though, a Marxist historian from the twentieth century, and for him the radicals are the heroes and the moderates are cowards. Complete flip."

Charlee arrived late, hair damp, sliding a book across the table like a poker chip. "Microfilm. Or whatever the modern equivalent is. The librarian pulled it for me because you texted me in all caps." Charlee sat down, eyed Gwendolyn's smoothie with open suspicion, and opened to a marked page. "Also, your all-caps text said the essay was due Monday, not next Friday."

"It's due Friday. Monday is when Ms. Rossi checks our thesis." Landon pulled the book toward him. "Which I don't have."

The three of them worked in a rhythm after that, the kind that only forms after years of shared classes and shared complaints. Charlee turned out to be a virtuoso of the index, tracing cross-references faster than Landon could request them, pulling threads: the moderate-praising account from the 1820s, the radical-sympathizing accounts from the twentieth century, a revisionist in between who claimed the whole Revolution had been a mistake. Gwendolyn played truculent opposition, poking at every draft sentence Landon muttered aloud, saying "prove it" with such regularity that he started saying it to himself.

By late afternoon the light through the window had gone from white to gold, and Landon had a page of notes that actually connected. Thiers and his moderate heroes on one side; the later historians and their radical heroes on the other; between them, not a straight line of improvement but a swinging pendulum, each writer partly answering the last. His thesis, when he finally said it out loud, was that the historians' politics and their narratives rose and fell together, which meant any "correct" account was written by someone standing somewhere. He liked it. He also knew it left him with the question he couldn't close: whether some account could be true anyway, standing nowhere, and he had to write "uncertain" in the margin in small letters, honest as a bruise. Gwendolyn said it was better than faking certainty. Charlee said the library closed in twenty minutes.

He packed slowly, shelving the books he hadn't checked out, leaving them spine-out on the return cart the way the sign asked. His notebook went in last, the "thesis??" page still visible under the new one, the old anger of it preserved under the day's work like a fossil under topsoil. At the door, Gwendolyn held it open with her foot.

"Monday, then," she said. "You'll say 'prove it' to yourself before I can."

"I already do," said Landon, and stepped out into the blue evening.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Air resistance slows real projectiles, so a thrown ball usually lands shorter than the calculation that ignores air resistance predicts.
story:
Tristan set the soup can on the kitchen table and measured the distance to the masking-tape line he'd stuck on the floor tiles. Ninety-two centimetres, though the problem on his notebook page insisted the ball should travel one metre and ten. He had separated the launch velocity into horizontal and vertical components exactly the way the textbook chapter showed, drawn the right triangle twice to be sure, and the arithmetic was clean. The calculator said 110. The can said 92.

His father drifted through for coffee and paused at the table, at the tape, at the bent plastic spoon propped against a stack of encyclopedias. "Physics homework?"

"Projectile motion," Tristan said. "You split the velocity into sideways and up-down parts. The sideways part never changes, so the ball goes the same distance every single time. It has to."

His father stirred his coffee slowly, watching the surface undulate, and said only, "Has to, huh," and carried the cup upstairs.

The demonstration was for Kenneth, who had texted in a panic on Thursday night. Their engineering club had entered a regional competition where teams built launchers to hit a target at a fixed distance, and Kenneth had done all his aiming calculations using the component method, the same clean math Tristan was now rehearsing at his kitchen table. On Saturday the launcher had fired six times, and all six balls had landed short. Not wildly short. Two or three centimetres, consistently, in a tight little cluster that Kenneth described as "offensively polite." The judges wanted each team to explain any gap between prediction and result, and Kenneth had until Tuesday to say something better than "we checked it four times."

Tristan found the explanation in his inbox at eleven that night, a message from Sabrina, who had watched the whole competition from the bleachers and, being Sabrina, had already written half a page about it.

You two treated the math like a prophecy, she wrote. I've been thinking about it since we got home. Your equations describe a ball flying through nothing, a vacuum, a world with no air in it. But there IS air in the gym. Air resistance slows real projectiles, so a thrown ball usually lands shorter than the calculation that ignores air resistance predicts. Nobody on your team factored it in because the chapter never does. It's not that your method failed. It's that it answered a slightly different question than the one you asked. Which is either a disaster or the best thing that's happened to your presentation, depending on how you frame it Tuesday.

From Sabrina's seat in the bleachers, Saturday had looked seismic at first, Kenneth going pale, Tristan's shoulders dropping as the sixth ball rolled to a stop short of the chalk ring. But she had watched Tristan carry the launcher to the car afterward with more care than he carried most things, checking the spring tension twice, and she suspected the failure was working on him the way a good argument did, quietly, rearranging the furniture.

He read the message three times, then set the phone face-down and stared at the tape line on the floor. His first instinct, held all weekend, had been that the calculation must be defended, that the method was a fortress and any shortfall was measurement error, a gust from the vents, a slightly dented ball. That position felt sturdy and, he now admitted, dishonest. The gap was real and it repeated itself. Sabrina's account wasn't an attack on the mathematics; it was a boundary drawn around the mathematics, a statement about where its jurisdiction ended. He had been arguing with the wrong opponent, as if protecting the formulas and describing the world were opposites, when really you needed both, held together, each correcting the other's excesses. His politics teacher called that a dialectic, two incomplete positions grinding against each other until something truer emerged from between them.

He thought about defending his old view anyway, out of pride. Then he picked up the phone.

"You were right about the air," he typed. "Kenneth has to say that part to the judges first, before he says anything else. We tell them the calculation gives the long distance, and the real ball lands shorter, and the difference is air resistance. Then we show the cluster. Six shots, all short by about the same amount. That's not failure, that's data."

Kenneth arrived Sunday afternoon carrying the launcher in a gym bag and a coffee can of practice balls under his arm. They ran the experiment again on the kitchen floor, this time measuring both distances, the predicted and the actual, and marking them with separate pieces of tape. The gap was smaller indoors than it had been in the gym, which Tristan recorded without yet understanding, a line in his notebook waiting for a reason. They drafted the presentation on the back of a supermarket receipt, crossed it out twice, and started over on proper paper.

"Say it back to me," Kenneth said, capping the marker. "The whole explanation, out loud."

"Air resistance slows real projectiles," Tristan said, "so a thrown ball usually lands shorter than the calculation that ignores air resistance predicts. Then I talk about what we still can't explain, and we go from there."

Kenneth tore off a fresh sheet and wrote the title at the top.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
story:
The recipe said to roast until the internal temperature hit sixty degrees Celsius, and Alexa, who had never cooked anything larger than a tray of cookies, trusted the recipe the way she trusted a syllabus. She had it propped against the flour canister, its margins already soft with butter from her thumb. Her mother was stuck at the hospital until eight, her father was driving back from her grandmother's, and the dinner for her grandmother's eightieth birthday had somehow landed on Alexa, seventeen years old, alone in the kitchen with a two-kilogram roast and a clock that read five forty.

"You're doing what?" Casey said on speakerphone, tinny against the counter. "You know your grandma. She'll notice if it's wrong. She noticed my shoes last time and didn't speak to me for an hour."

"She'll notice if it's raw, definitely," Alexa said. She slid the probe into the thickest part of the meat the way the internet had shown her, twenty minutes ago, in a video she had watched three times. "Matthew said his family does this every Sunday, so how hard can it be."

Matthew, texted, had sent back only a thumbs-up and the word "thermometer," which she found less reassuring than he probably intended. She set the oven timer anyway, because a deadline without a backup felt like walking a tightrope without a net, and by six twenty the probe read fifty-eight and climbing. The guests were arriving at seven. Her grandmother was intransigent about punctuality and, Alexa suspected, about roasts as well.

At fifty-nine degrees she stood with the oven door open, watching the number like a hawk. The recipe had a bromide at the bottom, "cook with love," which had annoyed her even on the first read; she preferred instructions that could be followed. When the display ticked to sixty she pulled the pan out, set it on the stovetop, and texted her mother a photo with the caption "nailed it." Then she covered the roast with foil, because the recipe said to rest it, and turned to the potatoes.

Her mother called at six forty, her voice half a hallway and half an apology. "It looks beautiful. Just don't cut into it yet, it needs to rest."

"It's resting," Alexa said. "It's a saint. It's resting so hard."

Ten minutes later she sliced off a thin end piece for herself, out of curiosity and nerves, and chewed it slowly at the counter while Casey talked about a party Alexa was missing. The meat was dense, the faintest bit grey at the edges, the pink gone from the center of the sample. Not ruined. But not what the recipe had promised either, and her grandmother had strong, unembarrassed opinions about overdone beef, delivered the way other people delivered weather reports.

She carried a piece of it next door, because Mr. Katz was the only person on the street who had ever cooked anything in front of her, whole chickens smoking on his grill in July. He was in his kitchen in a cardigan, and he listened with his head tilted, and when she finished he said only, "Carryover cooking. It keeps cooking after it leaves the heat. A big roast like that, the temperature can go up by several degrees while it rests."

Alexa stood in his doorway doing the arithmetic. Sixty at the oven, plus several degrees, resting under foil like a held breath. The recipe had told her a destination, not a route; it had given her a number without telling her the number would keep moving after she stopped steering. She thought of her college applications, pinned to the corkboard above her desk, each one a target temperature she had been chasing all year, and the uncomfortable thought arrived that pulling something out exactly at its stated number might not be the same as pulling it out done.

"Can I fix it?" she asked.

"Can't take the heat back out," Mr. Katz said. "But you can feed it to hungry people and learn for next time."

She went home and did the only thing left to do. She carved the rest thin, laid it on the good platter with the potatoes and the pan juices poured over everything, and set it in the middle of the table just as headlights swept the window. Her grandmother came through the door smelling of cold air and lilac, her cane clicking, and stopped in front of the platter with the expression of a customs officer. She took a slice, ate a bite, and Alexa waited, absolutely still, holding two truths in her head at once: that she had been wrong about the recipe, and that she understood now something the recipe had never thought to codify.

"It's a bit well done," her grandmother said. "The gravy saves it. Who taught you the gravy?"

"Nobody," Alexa said. "I just didn't take it off the heat too early."

Her grandmother looked at her for a long moment, then reached for a second slice.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence.
story:
Colton had tied his skates three times before Londyn found him on the bench by the skate rental counter. "You're early," she said, dropping onto the wood beside him. "Nobody's early for a first date. That's like being early for a test you didn't study for."

"I studied," Colton said. "I watched two videos about crossovers."

Londyn laughed, then didn't, because a girl came through the doors shaking snow off her jacket, and Colton stood up so fast his skate guard skidded across the floor. That was Roxanne, fifteen minutes early herself, which neither of them would admit to each other for another hour.

They went out onto the ice with the awkwardness of two people who had spent a week texting in complete sentences and now had to produce actual words. Colton fell once in the first five minutes, and Roxanne laughed in a way that made falling seem like a reasonable career. She was better than he was, it turned out, a year of Saturday lessons showing in her easy glide, and he followed her around the rink's slow outer loop while the lights turned the ice pink and then blue.

It was going well. That was the strange part, how well it was going, and Colton found himself ruminating on it even as it happened, turning the evening over like a stone in his pocket. He had spent so long deciding what kind of person to be on this date that he'd almost forgotten to check what kind of person he actually was.

Then he saw the other couple. They were near the boards on the far side, a boy from the grade above and a girl Colton recognized from his chemistry class, and the boy had her arm, had it the way you'd hold a dog that might run. Not guiding, not steadying. Gripping. When she tried to turn toward the music he pulled her back and her skate blades stuttered against the ice. She laughed, but it was a thin laugh, a laugh doing a different job than laughing.

"You see that?" Londyn materialized beside him, breath fogging. She'd been doing laps, instructor's kid posture, all efficiency.

"She grabbed him first," Colton said, uncertain even as he said it.

"Like this?" Londyn reached out and took Colton's forearm, firm but easy, the way you'd steer someone away from a puddle. Then she let go. "That's grabbing someone first. What he's doing is different. There's a word for it."

"Mean?"

"There's a real word for it. Physical dating violence. My cousin did a whole project on it last semester. She had this number that stuck with me." Londyn glanced over at the couple again. "In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about one in twelve US high school students who'd dated reported experiencing physical dating violence." She said it flat, like she was reading it off a card in her memory. "One in twelve. I kept thinking about how many people that is just in our grade."

Colton skated a slow circle around that fact, so to speak. One in twelve sounded small until you did the math on a cafeteria. And the boy wasn't a monster, probably; he was the guy who'd once helped Colton carry a table when no one else had bothered. People could be both things. Colton didn't know what to do with that, and the not knowing bothered him more than any answer would have.

Roxanne drifted back to them, cheeks red. "What are you two conspiring about?"

"Nothing," Colton said, and then, because the whole evening had been about being honest, or trying: "That guy. With the arm. Do you know them?"

Roxanne looked. "She's in my French class. She seems sad lately. Like, Tuesdays-sad, specifically." She paused. "Which is when they started dating."

They stood at the boards together, the three of them, watching the couple come around the loop. The boy's hand was on her arm again. Colton thought about saying something to him directly and could see, in advance, the whole conversation curdling into a shove on the ice. He thought about telling the girl, and imagined her face closing. He thought about doing nothing, which felt like its own kind of consent.

"I'm going to ask her to skate with us," Roxanne said. "Girls' lap. Whatever. He can't exactly object to that without looking like a complete creep."

"Is that interfering?" Colton asked. It was a real question, not a rhetorical one, and Roxanne seemed to hear it that way.

"It's inviting her to something," Roxanne said. "The rest is up to her."

She pushed off across the ice, and Colton watched her go. The rink's speakers moved on to a song he half knew. He didn't know if one in twelve included this girl, or if tonight's small rapprochement, three strangers orbiting toward one person, would matter at all by Tuesday. He only knew that the concrete fact of a hard hand on a soft arm was in front of him, and that someone was finally gliding toward it.

Colton looked at Londyn.

"Do we follow?" he asked.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
story:
Charles had folded his one good shirt three times on the bus, and by the time he reached Marlowe's Grill it looked like it had opinions of its own. He was twenty minutes early, which was either conscientiousness or desperation, and he took a booth near the window to wait. The restaurant smelled of coffee and grilled onions, and a woman he recognized as Ms. Teo, his old eleventh-grade English teacher, was reading a paperback two tables away. He slid down in the booth, unsure whether being seen rehearsing in public added to his gravitas or subtracted from it.

Kaylin arrived exactly on time, sliding into the opposite seat with a notebook. "Okay," she said. "You said on the phone you freeze up. So we use the STAR method. It answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result." She said it quickly, like handing him a tool rather than a lecture. "People who interview you don't want a feeling. They want a shape."

"Like a story with corners," Charles said.

"Like a story they can grade," Kaylin said. "Pick something real. Something that went wrong."

He picked the chemistry group project from last spring, the one where two of his three partners had stopped showing up and the third, Leanna, had quietly done half the work herself while Charles spent a week drafting emails nobody answered. He had always thought of that project as a failure with his name on it, the way a condemned house still has an address. Kaylin made him tell it twice. The first time it sprawled, full of grievance. The second time she held up four fingers and folded them down one at a time, and something in the telling tightened. Situation: three weeks, four people, one grade. Task: the lab report had to be finished regardless. Action: he stopped waiting for the absent two, split the remaining sections with Leanna, and called one partner's house when email failed. Result: they submitted on time, and the two who vanished were reported to the teacher, which he had hated doing.

"You hated it," Kaylin said. "Say that part too. Interviewers like a person who can do a thing he hates for a reason."

"I don't want to monetize my whole personality," Charles said, only half joking. "This is a bussing tables job."

"This is a first job," Kaylin said. "Everything after it will ask what you did in it."

The manager came out at four o'clock sharp, a heavyset man with a jaundiced, tired face and a pen he clicked like a metronome. He sat down across from Charles in the next booth over and asked the question Charles had been dreading in its exact form: "Tell me about a time things didn't go the way you planned." For a second his mind went white, the way a screen does before an image loads. Then he thought of Kaylin's four fingers. He laid the story out corner by corner, Situation to Result, and heard his own voice stay level, and noticed, with a kind of separate wonder, that the manager's pen stopped clicking somewhere around the Task.

"You reported your own group members," the man said.

"They hadn't done the work," Charles said. "And Leanna had. It wouldn't have been fair to her to pretend otherwise." He wondered, even as he said it, whether fairness was the real reason or just the respectable one, whether some part of him had simply wanted the thing finished.

Ms. Teo looked up from her paperback then, caught his eye, and raised her coffee cup half an inch, which was either a toast or just a hello. The manager wrote something on his clipboard. "Thursday and Friday nights, trial week," he said. "You start Thursday at five."

Afterward, at the door, Charles asked Kaylin whether she thought he'd gotten it because of the method or in spite of it. "Does it matter?" she said, but he found that for him it did, a little, the way it matters whether a lock opened because of the key or because the door was never locked. He stood on the curb holding his folded shirt, and through the window he watched Ms. Teo turn a page, and the manager carry a tub of dishes toward the kitchen, and the empty booth where a thing with corners had happened. "Thursday," he said to Kaylin. "Come after close and I'll buy you fries with my first shift's tips."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The overall equation for aerobic cellular respiration is C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy: glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water.
story:
Hudson had failed the cellular respiration quiz twice, and Ms. Takahashi had offered him a deal that felt more like a sentence: three days of his spring break at her sister's farm, helping with the greenhouse, and she would let him retake it. His mother had driven him out without asking a single question, which was its own kind of verdict.

The first morning he was handed a wheelbarrow and pointed at a compost pile that steamed faintly in the cold, like something alive. He was thinking about mitochondria, or trying not to, when a girl about his age came around the corner of the barn carrying a bucket in each hand. "You're the one here for penance," she said. "Ayanna. Ms. Takahashi is my aunt." He noticed she said it the way people mention a scar, casually, daring him to comment.

They worked badly together at first. He dropped a tray of seedlings; she told him the exact monetary value of each one; he told her that if she wanted to be propitiated he could apologize in Latin. She didn't laugh, but something around her mouth gave in slightly.

On the second day they walked down to the pond at the low end of the pasture, where the ice had retreated to a gray margin and the water lay flat and patient. Ayanna was explaining that the pond was hypoxic in winter, that the fish slowed down and the whole system held its breath, when Hudson, mostly to change the subject from his quiz, breathed out hard over the water and fogged it. "Where does that go," he said. "The carbon. In my breath. Like, where did it even come from this morning?"

"You breathe out carbon dioxide," Ayanna said. "Everybody knows that."

"Okay, but it was a granola bar an hour ago. It was a plant, like, last summer." He crouched at the edge, watching the fog of himself dissipate. Somewhere in him the equation began assembling itself, the way a phrase of a song returns without being summoned. Glucose and oxygen becoming carbon dioxide and water. Six of one thing, six of the other, like a receipt. "So I'm exhaling the granola bar," he said. "And the oxygen part, that came from the air, and it all got taken apart inside my cells, in the mitochondria, and turned into ATP, which is what my arms are using to hold me up right now." He looked at his own forearm as though it had betrayed classified information.

Ayanna was quiet long enough that he checked her face for mockery and didn't find any. "My aunt said you failed it twice," she said finally. "That was a solid two minutes of you not failing it."

That night, in the bunkhouse, he found a text from his friend Christian, sent at 7:41 with its usual disregard for his circumstances: "yo did you escape the farm yet. also my mom says hi. ALSO i looked up what you said about the pond thing and she wants to know if the plants around it undo what your breath does, like the pond is a mirror." Hudson typed back, "glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy. that's the whole thing. the plants basically run it backward and i still can't explain the middle part." Christian replied with a single thumbs up, which Hudson understood to be the emotional ceiling of their friendship.

He had been honest in the text. The equation sat in his mind clean and complete, but the middle, the winding path from glucose to ATP, the electron carriers, the way the mitochondria folded energy out of a sugar molecule like a magician producing an impossible length of scarf, remained half dark to him. On the third morning he told Ayanna so, leaning on the greenhouse bench while she pressed seeds into soil with a spatula she had decided was good enough. "I can say the equation," he said. "I can't walk it through the cell. There's a gap."

"Then stop trying to memorize the walk and draw the map," she said, and slid a scrap of butcher paper across the bench. He drew a glucose molecule as a lopsided hexagon, arrows branching and rejoining, the mitochondrion as a bean with a maze inside it. Twice he got a step wrong and she caught it, not kindly, and he crossed it out. The quiz was going to be multiple choice, which he suspected of being a pernicious comfort, the kind that let you recognize an answer you could never build yourself.

Driving home, his mother asked how it had gone, and he said the farm was fine, which was a lie of scale rather than of fact. What he did not say was that he had begun to suspect his two failures had been a kind of solipsism, an assumption that the material existed only inside the test, with no pond, no granola bar, no steaming compost at the other end of it.

He took the retake on Monday. Question fourteen asked for the overall equation, and beside it, for reasons he couldn't name, he sketched a tiny pond in the margin before writing C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy. Then he crossed the pond out, in case Ms. Takahashi thought he was mocking her sister, and went back to the mitochondrion, drawing the maze.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers popularized the '10,000-hour rule', though Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours.
story:
The garage smelled of cut grass and motor oil, and the one bare bulb overhead gave just enough light to read the chord chart taped to the wall. Savannah sat on an overturned milk crate with her mother's old guitar across her knees, pressing her fingers to the frets until the tips went white, then strumming. The sound was wrong in a way she couldn't yet name, thick where it should have been clean, like the notes were trying to coagulate in the air before they reached her ears.

"You're muting the B string," Syed said from the workbench, where he was supposed to be sorting screws for his father but was mostly watching her. "Your ring finger is leaning on it."

She adjusted, strummed again, and the chord rang out round and full. She laughed before she could stop herself. Two weeks of practice had produced exactly four chords, and that one clean E minor felt like finding water in a dry field.

"See, this is why it's pointless," Syed said. He picked up a screw, held it to the light, dropped it in the wrong bin. "My cousin read that Malcolm Gladwell book, Outliers, from 2008. It popularized the 10,000-hour rule. You need 10,000 hours to get good at anything. You're seventeen. There aren't enough hours left."

"Eighteen," Savannah said. "Since March."

"Fine, eighteen. Still too many hours." He swept a line of metal filings off the bench into his palm. "You should have started when you were six. I'm just being a pragmatist about it."

She played the E minor again, softer this time, listening to the way it faded into the quiet of the garage, past the dormant lawnmower, out toward the creek that ran behind the houses on this street. Through the open side door she could see the riparian tangle of willow and knotweed at the water's edge, green going gray in the late light.

That night she looked it up. Not because Syed had won, but because the number bothered her, sitting in her mind like a stone in a shoe. She found the Gladwell book at the library website, then found something else: an interview with a researcher named Ericsson, whose work the book had drawn on. Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, then closed the laptop and sat in the dark kitchen with her hands folded on the table.

The next afternoon she was back on the milk crate. Ms. Gill, the neighbor whose garage it technically was, came out with two glasses of iced tea and pulled up a lawn chair in the doorway. She was retired from teaching music at the middle school and had offered the space when Savannah's mother mentioned the apartment was too thin-walled for practicing.

"How's it going?" Ms. Gill asked.

"I'm trying to figure out if I'm wasting my time," Savannah said. "A friend says ten thousand hours is too many to start at my age. But I read this researcher, Ericsson, and he said quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours. So I'm trying to practice, like, better instead of just more." She winced at how it sounded coming out, a book report delivered to a lawn chair.

Ms. Gill sipped her tea and didn't answer right away. A cardinal landed in the willow by the creek and scolded something invisible. "Play me what you have," she said finally.

Savannah played the four chords in a slow loop, stumbling on the change from G to D, recovering, stumbling again. Her left hand ached at the base of the fingers where the tendons were learning to stretch. When she finished, the strings hummed against the strap button and went still.

"Here's what I heard," Ms. Gill said. "You sped up every time you got it right and slowed down every time you didn't. You're practicing being nervous." She set her glass on the concrete. "Try it at one speed, the boring speed, the whole way through. That's a quality. The hours will be whatever they are."

Savannah thought about Syed's cousin's arithmetic and about Ericsson's correction, and how neither one told her whether she'd ever be good, only how to hold the question. Maybe the hours were the wrong unit entirely; maybe they were only the frame around whatever you put inside them. She didn't know, and she suspected that not knowing was going to be a permanent condition of this particular endeavor. She set the metronome app on her phone to sixty, a beat plainer than her own pulse.

She played the loop again at the boring speed. Through the open door, the creek moved quietly under the willows, and Ms. Gill reached over and tapped the concrete once at the fourth beat of every measure, steady as anything.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Both countries gain from trade only if the exchange rate between the two goods falls between the two countries' own opportunity costs of making them.
story:
The Saturday market opened under a fog so evanescent that by nine it had burned off the blacktop entirely, leaving only the smell of wet canvas and fried dough. Elliot had been hired to stack Ms. Gauthier's honey jars and make change, nothing more, and for the first hour that was all he did, watching the apple farmer across the aisle glare at the sky. Rain was coming; the radio in the back of her truck said one o'clock, and everyone was trying to sell out before it arrived.

The apple farmer came over at half past nine, when the customers thinned. He wanted honey, four jars, and he wanted to pay with apples. "A basket of my Cortlands for two jars," he said, and Ms. Gauthier folded her arms and said no, three jars, because her time was not free and neither was her bees'. They stood in the narrow gap between the stalls, neither moving, while the clouds stacked up over the hardware store.

Elliot had been staring at his economics textbook all week, the chapters he was supposed to master before placement tests in the fall, and something about the argument snagged in his mind. He asked Ms. Gauthier, quietly, while she weighed out a pound of comb, what it cost her to make a basket of apples herself, if she ever did. She said she had six apple trees and no time for them, that a basket of her own apples cost her about three jars of honey in neglected hives. Then he crossed the aisle, bought a cider he didn't want, and asked the farmer the same question in a roundabout way. The farmer laughed and said apples were nearly free to him, that a basket cost him maybe one jar's worth of effort, if he counted at all.

Elliot sequester ed himself behind the honey table with a receipt and a pencil stub, and the numbers arranged themselves almost politely. If Ms. Gauthier made apples herself, a basket would run her three jars. If the farmer made honey himself, each jar would cost him a basket, so one basket cost him one jar of his own effort. Any trade between one jar and three jars a basket, and both of them came out ahead of doing everything alone. Below one jar the farmer lost; above three, Ms. Gauthier did. The farmer had asked for two, which sat square in the middle of the range, and Ms. Gauthier had refused it, which meant she was refusing a deal that still left her better off than her own orchard would. Or he had the numbers wrong. That possibility stayed open, and he held it carefully, not closing it.

Adriana watched him from the pastry stall where she worked, and it was she who noticed what he was doing, because she had spent the whole morning noticing him. She had her own deadline, a tray of almond croissants that would not survive the rain, and her own theory of Saturday mornings, which she called organized hedonism, taking pleasure on a schedule before the crowds and weather ruined everything. She came over under the pretense of buying beeswax lip balm and saw the pencil stub, the receipt covered in fractions, the two farmers still glaring. "You're doing the thing," she said. "The test-prep thing. You get a line between your eyebrows."

"I think they can both win," Elliot said, "and they're about to both lose." He told her the range, one jar to three, and how two sat inside it, and she said, "So go say that, before they'd rather be stubborn than dry." The first fat drops hit the canvas over their heads. Kayden, who had wandered over from the coffee cart with a broom he was supposed to be using, looked at the receipt and said, "That's comparative advantage," and then, when they stared at him, "We had it Tuesday. I only remember because it was on my birthday."

Elliot walked into the gap between the stalls with his receipt held like a hall pass. He said it plainly, that her own apples cost her three jars a basket, that his cost him one, that anywhere between those two numbers they both gained, and two was inside. The farmers looked at him, then at each other, and the apple farmer said, "Two and a half, then, and the young man takes the change in windfall apples." Ms. Gauthier said two and a quarter and a jar of last year's comb, and the rain came down in earnest while they shook hands on it.

Adriana counted what remained of the morning on her fingers: the croissants sold out by quarter to one, the honey table nearly bare, Kayden sweeping rainwater off the awning with the broom held flat like a squeegee. Elliot was still crouched behind the table, adding the morning's totals twice, because something in him would not let the numbers rest. Ms. Gauthier had known her own costs for thirty years; the farmer had known his; and still they had needed a teenager with a pencil to find the space between. She wondered whether he understood yet that he had not made the deal fair, only possible, and that the two and a quarter was still somebody's guess.

The truck doors slammed against the weather. Elliot folded the receipt into his back pocket without deciding whether the numbers had been exactly right, and carried the last crate of jars to the tailgate, where his hands slipped on the wet wood and he caught one jar an inch from the gravel. "Careful," Ms. Gauthier said. "That one's yours."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A mortgaged home is collateral for the loan, so if the borrower stops paying, the lender can foreclose, taking and selling the home to recover the debt.
story:
The foreclosure sign on the Hendersons' lawn had been there for six days before Kayla let herself look at it properly. She had walked past it twice a day on her way to the real estate office where she sorted listings after school, and each time she had read the bank's name and nothing else, the way you read a warning label on something you don't own. On the seventh day she stood at the edge of the Hendersons' dry grass, her bike still ticking behind her, and copied the sign's phone number into her notebook beside her list of questions. At the top of the list, underlined twice, was her own question: how much, actually, does a place cost.

She had taken the job at Marston Realty for money, plainly. Eight dollars an hour to shred expired listings and alphabetize buyer files, plus the occasional showing where she unlocked doors for people and then stood near the kitchen island pretending she was not there. But the files had captivated her more than she expected. There was a folder for everything: earnest money, escrow, and a fat one marked just "Pre-Qual." She had started reading them on her lunch break, half a sandwich in one hand, and what she found was that buying a house was mostly a long argument about who owed whom, and how much, and what happened if the owing stopped.

"You're the one who reads the files," said Imogen, who came in on Thursdays to use the copier because the library charged for printing. Imogen wanted to launch a zine about the town's vanished drive-in and had, so far, produced one page with a drawing of a hot dog on it. "So explain to me why the Hendersons have a sign from a bank on their lawn. Their house isn't for sale. I checked."

"That's the thing," Kayla said. "It kind of is." She turned the folder toward Imogen. "When they bought it, they didn't have the whole price, so the bank paid it and they pay the bank back every month. That's a mortgage. But the house is collateral for the loan. It backs it up." Imogen looked blank, and Kayla heard herself arrive at the sentence before she fully understood it. "If the borrower stops paying, the lender can foreclose. They take the house and sell it to get their money back."

Imogen chewed on this. "So the house is like a hostage."

"That's a terrible way to put it."

"Thank you."

Ms. Le, the agent whose desk sat nearest the files, had been half-listening with the expression of someone grading a recital. She was congenitally unable to leave an inaccuracy standing, and now she rolled her chair over. "Close," she said. "But you left out rent, which is most of what a girl your age will actually pay for years. Renting, you put down a deposit, usually a month's worth, and you get it back at the end if you haven't ruined anything. Buying, you need a down payment, a chunk of the price up front, and it's not coming back, because it's already yours, sunk into the house." She said the last part while looking directly at the folder in Kayla's hand, and something in her face made Kayla close it slowly.

That evening Kayla sat at the kitchen table with her mother, who was doing something complicated with envelopes. "Did you see the Hendersons put in a pool?" her mother said, too brightly. "Years ago. Remember the little waterfall."

"Mom." Kayla kept her voice flat, the way you handle a kettle you suspect is already hot. "What's our mortgage?"

The envelope-sorting stopped. Down the hall the dryer buzzed and nobody moved. Kayla watched her mother's hands, the way she squared the envelopes against the table edge twice, three times, and she understood that she had walked past her own warning label for months, the second job, the calls taken in the hallway, the word "refinance" pronounced quietly, as if volume were the problem. When her mother finally spoke, it was to say that the Hendersons' pool had been a mistake from the start, that nobody needed a waterfall, and Kayla let her finish because it seemed to cost her something to finish.

"It's not foreclosure," her mother said then, all at once. "We're two months behind and the bank sent a letter and I have a meeting, an actual meeting, with a person, on Thursday. That's all it is. That's all." She said it twice, which is how Kayla knew to believe it and also not to believe it completely, both at once, the way she believed the pre-qual folder and also the folder marked "Default."

On Thursday after school, Kayla unlocked a four-bedroom for a young couple and stood near the kitchen island while they counted their savings out loud, debating a down payment like it was a stone they were choosing to carry uphill. She wanted to tell them about deposits, about collateral, about how a house could be a home and a hostage in the same breath, and how she still couldn't say which one it was. Instead she handed them the disclosure packet and said, "Take your time."

When she locked the door behind them, she checked her phone. One text from her mother: a photo of the bank's lobby, and under it, "Still in the meeting."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: In a strike, employees refuse to work; in a lockout, the employer stops work by keeping employees out of the workplace.
story:
The automatic doors at Ferraro's did not open for Autumn on Tuesday morning, which was how she learned, before she learned anything else, that the store had stopped wanting her. A yellow sign was taped to the glass on the inside, backwards from her side, so she had to read it in reverse: CLOSED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. Beneath it, in marker, someone had written THANK YOU FOR YOUR PATIENCE, which struck her as optimistic, since nobody had been asked for any. She stood there in her green apron, the one she still had in her bag because the laundry had backed up, and waited for the doors to change their mind.

Delaney was sitting on the curb with a travel mug, coat zipped to her chin although it was September. "You too," she said, which was not a question. She nodded at the doors. "They did it at midnight. Chained the carts, changed the codes."

"I thought everyone was walking out today," Autumn said. "Delaney was passing out flyers about it at school. Strike vote, the whole thing."

"Vote was Thursday. We didn't pass it. We were still bargaining." Delaney took a long sip, the way people do when they want the pause to be noticed. "This isn't a strike, Autumn. This is a lockout. In a strike, we refuse to work. This is the other thing. They're keeping us out."

The distinction felt at first like a technicality, and then, as Autumn stood there with her useless apron, less like one. She had walked out once, in her head, rehearsing it at the register during slow hours, imagining the dignity of it. Being locked out had a different texture. It was like being broken up with by someone you had been planning to break up with first.

The union hall was six blocks east, above a dental office, and Delaney had a hand-drawn map because her phone battery had died, which she described as management's fault in a way Autumn chose not to interrogate. Inside, folding chairs circled a coffee urn the size of a small keg. Ms. Tse, who had negotiated the last contract and apparently every contract since the invention of groceries, was taping a schedule of picket shifts to the wall. She wore a lanyard with so many pins it could double as scale armor. Around her, a dozen workers argued about the pharmacy techs, who were on a different contract and had been told to report as usual, a rift Autumn could feel even without understanding it.

"Saturday," Warren said, materializing beside her with a clipboard. He went to her school; they had suffered through calculus together, an experience that had made them friends the way trench warfare makes friends. He was taking names for the picket line, and his handwriting was very neat, which somehow made it worse. "The whole point is we hold together on the wage floor. If they can drop starting pay, they can drop everyone's, eventually. It's like a lemma. You prove the small thing, and the big theorem follows." He said this as though it were reassuring. Autumn signed for Saturday and, after a pause, for Sunday too, and noticed Delaney watching her sign with an expression she filed away for later.

The later came fast. Ms. Tse called the room to order and laid out where bargaining had stalled: wages, yes, but also the scheduling clause, the one that guaranteed posted schedules two weeks out, the clause that had let Autumn take her Thursday labs and keep the job at all. Someone asked about unemployment insurance, and Ms. Tse said it varied by state and by circumstance, and that locked-out workers sometimes qualified and sometimes did not, and the word "sometimes" did more damage to the room's mood than any refusal could have. A man near the window said his wife was due in November. Nobody answered him, which was its own kind of answer.

Then the twist, when it arrived, wore a familiar coat. Through the window over the sink, where the union's dying ficus stood, Autumn watched her father's car pull into the lot across the street. He did not come in. He sat in the driver's seat with a legal pad on the steering wheel, and she understood, in one inchoate rush that she would spend the rest of the week trying to organize, that the company had brought him in on the management side. He did labor law. She had spent her whole childhood telling people proudly what he did without once asking whom he did it to.

She went down the metal stairs and across the lot. He rolled the window down before she reached it, which meant he had seen her coming, which meant he had known where she worked, which meant the legal pad was no accident.

"They haven't hired you in years," he said. "You picked the one grocery store in the county with a strong local."

"They picked me," she said. "You always say labor market, like it's weather. It isn't weather. People make it." It came out more cleanly than she felt it, which was the story of her whole relationship with him. He said he was doing a job, that someone would do it, that the lockout was lawful and the union knew it, that these things settled. She said nothing, because in her head she was hearing Delaney on the curb explaining the difference between walking out and being shut out, and understanding that her father was the shut.

Back upstairs, Warren asked if she was still good for Sunday. He had, she realized, a want of his own, and it wasn't the wage floor. He had crossed nothing, betrayed nothing, and yet he circulated among the locked-out workers with the energy of a boy trying to expiate a crime he hadn't committed, hungry to be counted on the right side of something, and she liked him more for it and trusted him exactly the same amount. She said she was good for Sunday. Delaney, by the urn, raised her mug half an inch.

The vote that night was whether to hold the line or return under the company's terms with the schedule clause suspended for ninety days, and Autumn raised her hand to hold, and watched a pharmacy tech raise hers to return, and did not hate her for it. The line carried. Outside, her father's car was gone, and the chalk marks on the lot said the space had been reserved, which struck her as the funniest thing she had heard all day, and she laughed at it alone on the stairs until Delaney came out and stood beside her without asking why.

"Picket starts at six," Delaney said. "Bring the apron. Nothing says what we are like the apron."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
Every August, Justine's grandmother left the porch radio tuned to a station that seemed to broadcast nothing but weather warnings for counties they had never visited, and this year Justine sat on that porch with her phone face-down on her knee, trying to decide whether to send a message she had already typed and deleted three times. The message was for Nyla. It concerned Colten. It had been drafted in the car on the way here, in the driveway, and now on the porch, and each version had been worse than the last, veering from what she suspected was cowardice into what she suspected was cruelty.

The facts were simple enough. They were all on the same summer club team, and in the last month Colten had missed practice twice without warning, once for a music festival and once, apparently, for nothing at all, and in the game on Saturday he had jogged through a rotation that Justine had called from the back line, and the other team had scored off it, and afterward Nyla had said, loudly, in the parking lot, "Colten, you always mess everything up," and Colten had gone very quiet in the particular way of a person deciding whether to be hurt or furious, and had chosen furious, and had not spoken to either of them since.

Justine had said nothing at the time. She had wanted to propitiate both of them, which she recognized, in retrospect, was not the same as helping either of them. Nyla was her oldest friend; Colten was newer, funny, the one who had taught half the team a card game during a rain delay. She remembered her mother once saying that her own strategy for family conflict was to agree with whoever had spoken most recently, and everyone in the family considered this hilarious, and no one had ever suggested an alternative.

Then, two nights ago, she had been half-listening to a podcast while cleaning her room, one of her grandmother's stations of a different kind, and a psychologist had said something she had rewound twice. He distinguished a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character. The host had repeated it back to him, testing it. You missed practice twice, that's a complaint. You always mess everything up, that's criticism. Justine had stood there with a damp cloth in her hand feeling as though someone had handed her a tool she should have been given years ago, along with a debit card and a locker combination.

So now, on the porch, she typed a fourth version. It began with the weather warnings, which she realized was a stall, and deleted that too. Her grandmother came out with two glasses of lemonade and set one down without comment, which was her method: she offered a beverage and then waited with the patience of a person who had outlived several decades of other people's drama. "Grandma," Justine said, "if you tell someone they did something wrong, how do you keep it from turning into a fight?" Her grandmother considered this while a man on the radio gravely announced a heat advisory for a county four hours north. "I don't know that you can," she said finally. "My sister didn't speak to me for two years over a casserole. But I will say the casserole was the actual subject, and she made it about me." She picked up her glass. "The casserole was dry. I said so. She heard that I was a person who despised her cooking, her house, her entire existence. Those are different sentences, Justine. She answered a sentence I never said."

Justine wrote that down on the back of a grocery receipt, because it felt like evidence, and because she had learned that her best thinking happened in paper form, away from the delete button. Then she typed the message and, before the fourth revision could begin, sent it. It read: Can we talk before practice Tuesday? Not about you being a bad teammate, because I don't think that. About the rotation on Saturday. I called it and you went the other way and I need to understand why before it happens again. Also you missed practice twice and I should have said something when it happened instead of saving it all up like a squirrel of resentment, which I realize is not a compliment to me.

Colten replied four minutes later with a single line: "a squirrel of resentment is the worst compliment I've ever received, see you Tuesday." Then a second line: "the festival was my cousin's band. I should've told coach. I didn't because it felt embarrassing. that part's on me."

Tuesday came, and the locker room was its usual theater of someone's lost shin guard and Nyla's querulous insistence that the cones had been moved, and Justine found Colten by the water station. He told her about the cousin's band, which was, by his account, a populist phenomenon in their small city, beloved precisely by the people no radio station would play, and he'd felt he couldn't explain skipping an elite club practice for them. She told him that when she'd called the switch rotation, she'd seen him look over and keep jogging straight, and asked if he hadn't heard her. He said he'd heard her and thought she was wrong, and had decided in the moment not to switch, and had not mentioned this decision to her, which, now that he said it out loud, he could hear was its own kind of decision to be a bad teammate, without anyone saying it.

"You didn't miss practice twice because you're a bad person," Justine said. "You missed practice twice. That's the whole sentence." He nodded slowly, the way people nod at things they intend to repeat later to themselves. Nyla appeared at the door with the cones, watched them for a moment, and said, to the room in general, "If you two are done, some of us are trying to run a drill." Colten looked at Justine, and Justine looked at the clipboard in her hand, and there was still the whole problem of Nyla, who had never in her life been handed a specific sentence instead of a general verdict, and might not want one. "Tuesday," Justine said. "Or Thursday. She gets the next slot." Colten picked up a cone and said, "Bring a casserole."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Encapsulation means hiding a class's data behind methods, so other code can use the object without depending on how it stores its data.
story:
The convention center smelled like floor wax and burnt coffee, and by nine in the morning Makayla had already traced the same forty lines of Java three times. Their robot, a squat thing with a claw arm the team called Pincher, sat dead on the practice table while the autonomous code refused to run. The regional competition started in an hour, and the fault was somewhere in her Robot class, which she had written in a hurry the week before with all its fields public: speed, heading, and the position of each motor, all sitting out in the open where anyone's code could reach in and change them.

"I only changed one thing," Billy said, hovering at her shoulder with a printed stack of his driving code. "I changed position from a double to an int, because the encoder library wanted whole numbers. That's it."

"That's it," Makayla repeated. Somewhere down the aisle, another team's robot cleared a wall of cups and its members shouted. She scrolled through the file and saw the damage spread like a crack through glass: Billy's driving code read position and divided by it; Treyton's autonomous code rounded it; the telemetry display, which someone had written in October, expected it to be a decimal and now printed garbage. Every piece of the team's code depended on exactly how her class stored its data, and she had let them.

Treyton dropped into the folding chair beside her, still holding the cash box he'd carried since the fund-raiser. He'd appointed himself team treasurer and took the role seriously, in the way of someone who had recently learned the word fiduciary and enjoyed saying it. "I have a fiduciary duty to this money," he announced, counting out their pizza budget. "Nobody touches the box except through me. That's the whole point of a treasurer. You want five dollars, you ask me, you don't reach into it."

Makayla stopped scrolling. She looked at the cash box, then at her code, and something shifted in her head so quietly she almost missed it. "Say that again," she said.

"About the five dollars? I was being serious, I have receipts."

"No, the part where nobody reaches in." She was already opening a new file. She rewrote the Robot class from the top, but this time she made every field private, sealed off where no other code could touch it, and wrote small public methods instead: getPosition, getSpeed, setPosition. If Billy wanted the position, he would call a method and get whatever she chose to give him. The methods were the door; the fields were locked in the back.

Billy, watching over her shoulder, demurred when she told him to change his driving code. "It'll take too long, we compete in forty minutes." But she showed him that his code only needed one edit, swapping the direct read for a call to getPosition, and the rest could stay exactly as it was. Then, to prove the idea, she did something reckless on purpose: she changed position back to a double, deep inside the class, and hit compile. Nothing else broke. Billy's code still ran, Treyton's still ran, the telemetry printed clean numbers, because none of it depended anymore on how she stored her data. It all went through the methods, and the methods kept working.

"It's called encapsulation," she said, mostly to herself, reading the word off a forum post she'd found at the bottom of her search results. She wrote a quick test method before she let herself relax, a few lines that created a Robot, set its speed, checked that the getter returned the right value, and printed pass in small letters. It felt strange and formal, like signing her own name to prove she existed, but when the word pass appeared she understood why people did it. The class was no longer just hers; it was something she could hand over.

They made it to the practice match with eleven minutes to spare. Pincher drove crooked, because Billy's turning constant had been wrong since October, but it drove. Treyton counted out pizza money with the solemnity of a bank teller, and when the announcer called their school's name, Makayla closed her laptop, resting one hand on the lid. On the screen behind her reflection, the test still read pass.

"Same time next Saturday?" Billy asked, coiling the battery cable.

"Bring your own five dollars," Treyton said, and snapped the cash box shut.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Countering is when one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, keeping both visible to the audience.
story:
Paige taped the floor plan to her grandmother's carpet with painter's tape, marking out the stage in the long living room between the piano and the bay window. Her grandmother had gone to bridge club, and the house was theirs until five. Blair arrived first with a duffel bag of props, then Maite, who had the script rolled in her back pocket like a permit.

The one-act was called "The Long Table," and Mr. Rosen, the retired drama teacher from across the street, had lent Paige his battered directing binder when she told him she'd won the spring festival slot. "The blocking is the whole first week," he'd said on his porch, tapping the binder. "Everything else is decoration." She'd read the binder twice on her bed, but reading was not the same as standing in a room with two actors who both wanted the window light.

"Start on page four," Paige said, sitting on the piano bench with the script. "Blair, you cross to the table. Maite, you stay planted."

They ran it. Blair walked from the armchair to the table, and Maite, standing at stage left, turned to face her, which put her body flat against the window. The afternoon glare took her face. In the mirror over the fireplace, where Paige had learned to check the audience's view, Maite had become a silhouette with no expression at all.

"Maite, I lost you," Paige said. "Try again."

They ran it four more times. Every time Blair crossed, Maite turned after her and vanished into the light, a black cutout with a voice. On the fifth run Maite stopped mid-line. "I'm not doing anything wrong," she said, not angrily, but with the flatness of someone who suspected she was being accused. "She walks, I watch her. That's the scene."

"I'm not trying to impugn your instincts," Paige said. "Something's happening that I don't have a word for yet."

Blair dropped into a kitchen chair and spun it once with her foot. "Maybe I shouldn't cross."

"You have to cross. The whole scene is her leaving and you deciding to follow." Paige pulled Mr. Rosen's binder onto her lap and flipped past the diagrams she'd already studied, the ones with arrows for entrances. In the back, in a section she'd skimmed, she found a hand-drawn sketch: two stick figures, one mid-cross, the other tilted a few degrees the opposite way. Underneath, in his cramped handwriting: "Countering." The note said that when one actor crosses, the other shifts position to balance the stage, keeping both visible to the audience. Paige read it three times, then looked up at the taped rectangle on the carpet.

"It's called countering," she said. "When you cross, she doesn't turn to face you. She angles the other way, a few steps downstage, so the stage balances and the audience can see both of you."

Maite squinted at the sketch. "So I move away from her instead of toward her."

"Try it."

Blair got up, and they ran page four again. Blair crossed to the table, and Maite took two unhurried steps downstage right, angling her shoulders away from Blair's path. In the mirror, both of their faces were open. The window light fell between them instead of behind one of them. It looked, for the first time, like a scene someone had designed on purpose.

"Again," Paige said, and they ran it twice more, until the movement stopped feeling like an instruction and started feeling like Maite's own idea, a small refusal that read as pride.

At four thirty Mr. Rosen crossed the street with his newspaper and stood in the doorway with permission from nobody, which was how he operated. He watched one full run in silence. When it ended, he said, "Who told you about countering?"

"Your binder. Page ninety."

"Huh." He folded the newspaper under his arm. "Most people never get that far. Most people direct with their ego and call it vision." He looked at Maite, still holding her downstage angle, and then at Blair, half-seated on the table's edge, which was not in any diagram. "The chair on the table is a bellicose choice, Ms. whoever-you-are."

"It reads as defiance," Blair said.

"It reads as a fire hazard at festival," Mr. Rosen said, but he was almost smiling. He told Paige the pacing in the middle dragged, that her closing monologue was shaping up as a peroration the audience would hear as a lecture unless she cut two lines, and that he would want tickets. Then he went home.

After he left, Paige sat back down at the piano bench with the script and a pencil. She wrote "cut two lines, which two?" in the margin, and underlined the question, because she did not know yet whether the ending should argue or simply stop. Maite and Blair were in the kitchen arguing about whether the table needed a cloth, their voices carrying through the old house the way voices did, arriving from everywhere at once. Paige read the last page twice, then called out, "From the top, no stopping."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884.
story:
Nolan had named his science fair project "Push Me, Pull You," which Abigaelle said sounded less like chemistry and more like a yoga studio, and which Rhiannon said sounded exactly like a yoga studio, in a tone that suggested this was a compliment. The project itself stood on a folding table in the atrium of the science museum: three sealed tubes of cobalt chloride solution, a bowl of ice water, a kettle that a museum aide had agreed to plug in behind the safety partition, and a hand-lettered sign reading DO NOT TOUCH, EXCEPT YOU, WE MEAN THE JUDGES.

The tubes were pink, all three, a color Rhiannon had described that morning as "Pepto-Bismol after a hard week." Nolan dropped one into the ice bath and set another into the kettle's warmth, then turned to the third and did nothing at all, because a control was a control, even when a control looked torpid next to its busy siblings. He waited. Waiting was the part of chemistry class that had beguiled him least, until this year, when equilibrium had turned waiting into the whole point: a reaction that never finished, only settled, then lurched when you changed its conditions.

The cold tube faded toward a deeper rose. The warm one shifted, slowly, toward a duskier violet. "It's like the molecules voted," Nolan said when Rhiannon wandered over from her own table, where she was demonstrating something involving magnets and a look of perpetual suspicion. "You cool it down, and the reaction slides one way. You heat it, it slides back the other. It's not confused. It's compensating."

"Compensating for what?"

"Me. For me being a menace with a kettle."

Ms. Esposito, who taught chemistry at the high school and had been drafted into judging, arrived at his table with a clipboard and the mild smile of someone who already knew how the demo worked. She watched the tubes, asked him to predict what the warm one would do if he returned it to room temperature, and nodded when he got the direction right. Then she asked the question he had not prepared for. "Do you know who Le Chatelier was?"

Nolan opened his mouth, found nothing in it, and closed it again. Beside him, Rhiannon made a small delighted noise, the noise of a friend watching a trapdoor open under someone else.

"He's the principle guy," Nolan said. "Le Chatelier's principle. That's the rule I'm using. The one about how equilibrium shifts when you change temperature." This was true and also, he could feel, completely insufficient, the way saying "Einstein was the relativity guy" was true and completely insufficient. Ms. Esposito did not rescue him. She said, "There's a wall of chemists down the corridor, past the dinosaur gift shop," wrote something on her clipboard, and moved on to Abigaelle's table, where something involving yeast was about to embarrass everyone.

"You have a gap," Rhiannon said. "A large, French-sounding gap."

"I have a research opportunity." Nolan set the torpid control tube back in its rack, promised the boy guarding his table, a neighbor's kid paid in soda, to keep the kettle away from the sign, and went down the corridor, past the gift shop, past a shelf of plush tyrannosaurs in scarves, to a long panel of portraits under the heading CHEMISTS WHO CHANGED EVERYTHING AND LOOKED FAIRLY TIRED DOING IT.

Le Chatelier turned out to be one of them. The panel gave him a sober mustache and two sentences: the principle was named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884. Nolan read it twice, partly because the information deserved it and partly because a family of four was trying to read over his shoulder and he felt briefly, absurdly, proprietary. Stated it. Not discovered it like a hidden cave, not invented it like a machine; stated it, the way you'd state a rule of a game everyone had been playing badly for centuries without naming the rules.

He walked back to the atrium composing sentences. The principle was named after Henry Louis Le Chatelier, a French chemist, and he stated it in 1884. That was the whole fact. It refused to become more than it was, and there was something he liked about that, a fact that sat still while you circled it, though he could not have said whether that was a property of the fact or of him.

The judge with the strongest opinion turned out to be a retired chemical engineer with reading glasses on a chain, who came by at three o'clock, watched the pink tube sink into the ice, and asked the same question Ms. Esposito had. Nolan gave his two sentences. The engineer looked at him over the glasses. "And do you understand it, or did you memorize the plaque?"

"Both," Nolan said. "The understanding is newer." He lifted the violet tube from the kettle, held it in the air between the bowl and the bath, and let it cool in his palm while the color crept back toward rose, undecided, going somewhere anyway. "Watch this part," he said. "This is my favorite part, and I can't fully explain it, so you're getting honesty instead."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: A 2002 study led by Richard Seager argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters.
story:
Morgan spread the ocean current map across the flat top of a concrete block at the edge of the quarry, weighting two corners with chunks of limestone so the June wind couldn't take it. The water below was the green of old bottle glass, cold even in summer, and she had chosen it because Rylee said the quarry was the only place in three counties where you could think without anybody's mother offering you snacks. Her presentation was due Tuesday. Ms. Clarke had assigned each student one claim from the unit and told them, with the enthusiasm of a woman who had read the same textbook for eleven years, to defend it. Morgan's claim: the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe.

She had believed it the way she believed that water drains counterclockwise, which was to say completely and without ever having checked. The textbook had a diagram, an orange ribbon curling up the Atlantic like a warm scarf, and beneath it a sentence she had underlined in yellow. Then Aydin had ruined everything in the library on Thursday by sliding into the seat across from her with the particular grin of someone holding a knife.

"Read this," he said, and turned his laptop toward her. "It's a 2002 study led by Richard Seager. It argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters."

She had said something dismissive about the internet, and he had pointed at the journal name, and she had gone quiet in the way that meant he was winning. Now, at the quarry, she had both sources in front of her, the textbook open to its diagram and a printout of the study folded into quarters, and she was trying to hold them together in her head the way you hold two ropes you intend to braid.

Rylee arrived carrying a cooler and an inflatable flamingo, which she introduced as her editorial consultant. She flopped onto a slab of slate and looked at the map. "So which is it? Is Europe warm because of the current or not?"

"That's the wrong question," Morgan said, and immediately heard how it sounded, like a graduate student defending a thesis on jurisprudence nobody had asked about. "Sorry. I think it's more that both things are true at once, and the study is saying the current isn't the main thing, the winds and the heat the ocean stores over summer are. But the current does something. Just not most of it."

"That's the least satisfying answer I've ever heard."

"I know. It's also the honest one." Morgan traced the orange ribbon with her finger, then the westerlies above it, the arrows crossing each other like the top layer of a weave. The sun moved off the high rock face and reached the water, and the green brightened to something almost turquoise near the far wall where the old crane cables still hung rusted.

That night she sat at her desk and wrote an email to Ms. Clarke, because it seemed cowardly to change her whole presentation without warning and braver to say it directly:

Dear Ms. Clarke,

My claim was that the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. I want to keep the topic but change the angle. There's a 2002 study led by Richard Seager that argued winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters. So my report will be about why the textbook version survived so long when the evidence pointed another way, and what the current does account for, which I'll admit I haven't fully sorted out yet. I would rather hand you something with a gap in it that I can see than something airtight and wrong.

Morgan

She read it four times, winced at the last sentence, kept it anyway, and hit send before she could turn into a person who drafted emails forever.

On Tuesday she stood at the front of the room with the same map, the corners now weighted with erasers. Aydin sat in the second row looking ebullient, ready to gloat or to back her up, she honestly couldn't tell which. She explained the ribbon first, gave the textbook its due, then laid the study over it. "Here's what I can't resolve," she said. "If the winds and the stored summer heat do most of the work, the warm current still matters some, and nobody in what I've read agrees on how much. So I'm going to give you both and the gap between them, and the gap is real."

Ms. Clarke was writing something on her clipboard. Rylee, in the back, raised the inflatable flamingo's head above her desk like a puppet offering silent support, and Aydin leaned forward and said, "So the warm scarf theory is dead?"

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: German capitalizes every noun, not only names, which helps a reader of a German article spot the nouns in a sentence at a glance.
story:
Mr. Rajapakse had left the article clipped to a manila folder on the reserve shelf: a short piece from a German regional paper, three paragraphs long, with a note in red pen saying Levi would summarize it aloud, in his own words, at the start of Monday's class.
