Levi carried the folder to the back table by the window, where Keisha was already sitting with her chemistry notes and Dante was eating sunflower seeds out of his pocket despite the signs forbidding food.

He read the first sentence and stopped. "Why are there capitals everywhere? Look. Der Bürgermeister. Der Kassierer. It's like half the words are names."

"Maybe they are names," Dante said, cracking a seed against his thumb.

"No, the second one's a job. The guy who ran the money. It says he took off with it." Levi ran his finger along the line. Something about the pattern bothered him, so he did what he always did with a problem: he counted. He marked every capitalized word in the paragraph, then went back and looked up three of them in the dictionary at the end of the table. Bürgermeister, mayor. Kassierer, cashier. Gemeinderat, town council. None of them were names. All of them were things, people, objects. He marked the lowercase words next and looked up two of those. Und, and. Nach, after.

"Every single thing-word starts with a capital," he said. "Not just the names. The mayor, the cashier, the money, the town, the vote. All of it."

Keisha leaned over, abandoning her notes. "So if you're reading, you can just see the nouns? They stand out on the page?"

"Like they're in bold." He turned back to the beginning and read the first sentence again, and this time the shape of it came through: the capitals marked out who did what to whom, a skeleton holding the sentence up while the little connecting words hung off it. He still could not tell what the sentence meant, exactly, but he could see its structure for the first time, the way he could see the framing of a house before the siding went on.

The article itself, once he worked through it with the dictionary, was better than he had expected. A town treasurer had absconded with forty thousand euros from the festival fund, and the town council was split about whether to hold a plebiscite on dissolving itself and merging with the larger town down the valley. The paper quoted one councillor calling another bellicose, which the dictionary glossed as quarrelsome, warlike. Levi wrote the three English words in the margin of his notebook because he liked them, then felt slightly dishonest about it, since he would be claiming them as his own on Monday.

Summarizing aloud was the hard part, and that was why he had asked Keisha and Dante to sit with him. He tried it twice and both times he lapsed into translating sentence by sentence, which Mr. Rajapakse had said was not a summary. "A summary says what happened," Levi said. "It doesn't say what the article said."

"So say what happened," Dante said.

Levi put the article face down on the table. "A cashier stole money from the town festival fund and disappeared. The council argued about whether to let the people vote on merging with the next town over. One of them called another one quarrelsome." He paused. "That's it. That's the whole thing, three paragraphs."

"It took you two hours," Keisha said.

"It took two hours to know what to leave out." He turned the article over again and looked at the rows of capitals, solid and regular, nouns standing in their places like fence posts. He would get up in class on Monday with the paper turned face down, and if Mr. Rajapakse asked him how he had managed it, he would say what he had actually done, which was count the capitals and look up the ones that repeated. He was not sure that was the proper way to learn a language. He was not sure it was the wrong one, either, and he had decided at some point during the counting that he did not mind not being sure, because the sentence on the page had held still for him either way.

"Once more," Keisha said, checking the clock above the periodical rack. "From the top. And this time don't stop at the part with the money."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
story:
Kevin had promised the gallery committee a savanna at dusk, and by Thursday afternoon the promise was going badly. The elephant he had painted in the foreground was the same gray across its whole back, one flat mix of black and white he had toned in a single cup, but on the canvas it refused to behave. Against the burnt orange of the dry grass the gray looked faintly blue, almost cold, while up near the shoulder, where the animal met the violet shadow of the acacia tree, the same gray turned warm, almost rosy. He stepped back to the sink counter and looked at it from a distance, then walked close again, as if the fault might be in his eyes at a particular range.

Koen was glazing a bowl two easels over, and Kristopher was supposed to be lettering the exhibit labels but had spent twenty minutes cutting a stencil of a bird instead. "Your elephant's two colors," Kristopher said, not looking up. "Left side's bluer. Did you mix twice?"

"I mixed once," Kevin said. "Same cup. Go look at the palette." The smear on the palette was neutral, honestly neutral, and he held the wooden edge up beside the canvas so Kristopher could see it. Kristopher came over, wiped his hands on his apron, and squinted. "That's weird," he said, which was the most anyone had committed to anything all afternoon.

Kevin's first instinct was to fix it. If the gray looked blue against the orange, he could warm the paint there until it matched what he wanted, and he actually squeezed a thread of raw sienna onto the palette before stopping himself. The trouble was that he did not know what he wanted. He had read somewhere, or half remembered reading, that museum restorers worried about this exact problem when they filled losses in old paintings, that a patch matched under the lamp could betray the whole surface under gallery light. And there was a second trouble underneath the first, the one he did not say aloud: the gallery committee had not asked for an elephant at all. They had asked for a savanna. He had added the animal because the empty plain felt like it was disenfranchising something, though he could not have said what, and now his one act of invention was arguing with itself.

Mr. Taylor came through on his rounds with his coffee, paused at the easel, and did the thing Kevin most dreaded, which was to say nothing for a long time. "The grass is good," Mr. Taylor said at last. "The tree is good. What's troubling you about the elephant?"

"The gray changes. Same paint."

Mr. Taylor nodded once, the way he did when a student had found a real problem, and went to the shelf behind the drying rack. He took down a battered paperback, its spine held with tape, and put it on Kevin's stool without opening it. "Chapter three," he said, and moved on toward the print room. That was all. Kevin would have preferred almost anything else, including being told the elephant was a gratuitous addition and should be sponged off.

He sat on the stool and found chapter three. The book was older than the classroom, a translation of a nineteenth-century French text on color, and the chapter described experiments with gray patches on colored grounds. The chemist who wrote it, Michel Eugène Chevreul, had published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. Kevin read the sentence twice, then held his thumb over the word complement and tried to reconstruct it from the plates opposite. A gray on orange ground drifted toward blue. A gray on violet ground drifted toward yellow and warm. He looked up at the elephant, and the elephant, smug and enormous, confirmed both.

"Listen to this," he said, and Koen and Kristopher gathered, leaving fingerprints on the book's margins. Kevin read the sentence aloud, 1839 and all, and Kristopher frowned. "So your paint didn't change."

"The paint didn't change," Kevin said. "The painting did." It sounded like a line from a fortune cookie, but it was true, and saying it made something settle in him. He was not being sloppy. He was being shown a law.

The decision he faced was smaller than the discovery but harder. He could neutralize the shift, adjusting the gray zone by zone so the elephant read as one animal, which would mean painting against what the eye actually saw. Or he could let the shift stand, and the elephant would belong to its savanna in a way he had not planned, cooler where the land burned, warmer where the shadow cooled, an animal that could not be lifted out of its ground without changing. He thought about the restorers again. They matched the paint, but the paint was never the point. The painting was the point.

He picked up the brush with the sienna still loaded in it, held it over the cool flank, and set it back down on the tray. Then he cleaned it under the tap, watching the water run gray, then clear. Koen was watching him. "You're leaving it?"

"For now," Kevin said. "Ask me at the opening."

Kristopher laughed and went back to his stencil, and the room went quiet except for the fan and the small sounds of the brush on paper. The elephant stood in the dusk Kevin had made for it, gray in two directions at once, and outside the tall windows the real light was also failing, also going orange on one side of everything and violet on the other.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: Sonata form has three main sections: the exposition presents the themes, the development works them through other keys, and the recapitulation brings them back.
story:
Thomas had three sticky notes flattened inside his jacket pocket, and he kept checking that they were still there the way other people checked for tickets. Green for the exposition, yellow for the development, blue for the recapitulation. He had written the words himself, printing them small and square, because printing felt safer than cursive, as if the block letters could codify something he only half understood.

"Exposition, development, recapitulation," Preston had said that afternoon, reading off Thomas's notes in the music room. "You actually memorized all three?"

"It's the sonata form," Thomas said. "The exposition presents the themes, the development works them through other keys, and the recapitulation brings them back."

"Sounds like immunology. First exposure, then the thing mutates, then your body recognizes it again."

"That's not how immunology works," Jazmin said, without looking up from her own score.

"That's exactly how it works," Preston said, and neither of them settled it.

The concert hall was warmer than the November street, and it smelled of carpet and old varnish. Mr. Koné, who taught theory on Tuesdays and had arranged the tickets, had given them seats in the third row. "Mark what you hear, not what you expect," he had told Thomas on the way in, which Thomas had taken as a kind of permission. The lights dimmed. The pianist, a small woman in grey, sat down without ceremony, and the first movement began before Thomas had his green note fully peeled off the backing.

He pressed it against his knee, not the seat, because Preston had pointed out that sticky notes left on velvet might get them thrown out. The opening theme was easy to follow, a tune that swung upward and then folded back down like a question rephrasing itself. He waited for a second theme, and when it came, lighter and in a different colour, he held the green note a little higher on his knee, ready. The music turned. It turned again, harder, and the melody he knew started breaking apart and traveling somewhere minor and unsettled. Yellow, he thought. This is the yellow part. He smoothed the note onto his knee and felt briefly, absurdly proud, like a navigator who had spotted land exactly where the chart said it would be.

Then came the trouble. The opening theme returned, and Thomas reached for blue, but it returned wrong, in the other key, the second theme's territory, and he froze with the note halfway off his knee. Jazmin leaned over. "Not yet," she whispered. "It's still working them through other keys. It's come back but it hasn't come home." He put the blue note back in his lap, and his ears did something strange then, something he had never asked them to do: they listened forward instead of backward. He was not waiting for pretty tunes anymore. He was tracking a negotiation.

When the true return finally came, both themes together, the first one grounded in its own key at last, Thomas pressed the blue note down and felt his face go hot. He had almost marked it a full minute early. The movement ended, and the applause came up around them like weather, and Preston leaned across Jazmin to mutter, "Okay, the immunology thing holds. It recognized it and everything."

Afterward, in the lobby with its chandeliers and its querulous crowd of old subscribers complaining about the alto in the second half, Mr. Koné found them by the coat check. "Well?" he said. He looked at Thomas's knee, where the three notes still sat in a neat row, green, yellow, blue, their order unbroken but their spacing, Thomas realized, all wrong. There was a long gap between green and yellow and almost none between yellow and blue, because he had misjudged when the working-through began.

"I marked the recap late the first time," Thomas said. "The theme came back but it wasn't the recapitulation yet. It came back in the wrong key."

Mr. Koné nodded slowly. "And how do you know when it is right?"

Thomas looked down at the three notes. "I don't, yet. Not for sure. Tonight I guessed and Jazmin caught it. Next time maybe I'll catch it myself."

"In that case," Mr. Koné said, and held out his hand, "give me the yellow one. You've earned a souvenir, and I've earned proof." Thomas peeled it off his knee and set it in the teacher's palm, where it stuck at a slight angle, still faintly warm.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, the closest relatives of the person who died sit shiva, a mourning period of seven days that begins after the burial; the Hebrew word shiva means seven.
story:
Aidan hadn't been to his grandfather's house in two years, and now he was going there for the second time in a week. The first time had been the funeral, the lawn full of folding chairs, the rabbi's voice thin against the wind off the lake. This time his mother drove with a casserole balanced on her knees, and the littoral road unrolled beside the grey water where his grandfather had once taught him to skip stones.

He had called Raphael the night before, awkward about it, because Raphael's family was Jewish and Aidan's was only half so, and only on the dead side. "What do I do," he'd asked. "What do I bring?"

"Food," Raphael said. "You don't bring flowers. People bring food because nobody feels like cooking." There was a pause, the sound of Raphael's sister arguing somewhere behind him. "They'll probably sit shiva."

"What's that?"

"Mourning. The closest relatives sit shiva for seven days, and it starts after the burial, so right after the funeral." Raphael said it the way he explained offside rules in soccer, patient, unimpressed. "Low stools, mirrors covered. You just show up and let them talk."

"Seven days. Why seven?"

"Shiva means seven. That's all it is." Another pause. "Wear something with a collar."

In the car now, his mother kept adjusting the casserole as if it were an argument she could win by placement. "Your grandfather would have hated all the fuss," she said. Aidan didn't answer. He was thinking about the last summer he'd spent here, fourteen years old, when he'd told his grandfather he was bored and asked to go home early. His grandfather had driven him to the bus station without complaint. Aidan had been carrying that culpability around for three years without naming it, and now there was nobody left to absolve.

The house had changed. Somebody had draped sheets over the mirrors, and the low chairs had been arranged in a half circle in the living room: his grandfather's sister, his two uncles, his cousin Helen, all sitting lower than everyone else, like judges at a trial conducted at ankle height. Aidan stood in the doorway holding the casserole and understood, suddenly, that his mother should be in one of those chairs. She was the daughter. She was standing anyway, refilling cups, and he couldn't tell whether she had chosen that or simply hadn't been asked.

Helen came over. She was nineteen and had cried recently enough that her face still had the shape of it. "You brought food," she said. "Good. There's so much food it's becoming a problem. The jello salad from the Bernsteins has basically coagulated into one solid object. Uncle David wants to photograph it."

"It's like a museum piece," Aidan said, and she laughed, a real laugh that surprised them both, and covered her mouth as if laughter had escaped custody.

He sat with the uncles for a while. They told the story about the time his grandfather had sailed through a storm because he refused to admit the forecast, and then told it again with better details, and Aidan realized the repetition was the point, that the story was being handled like a stone being turned over and over in the pocket of the family. He added the detail about the stones, how his grandfather could get six skips off a flat one, and his uncle Sam said, "Six, that's generous, he counted four," and for a moment they argued about it with real feeling, and the argument was a kind of grief he could participate in.

Later he found his mother in the kitchen, alone, running water over a dish that was already clean. "Mom. Shouldn't you be sitting out there?"

She turned the dish over. "I haven't been to temple since I was your age. I don't know the prayers. I'd be sitting there like a guest at my own father's funeral." Her voice stayed level in the way that meant it was costing her. "Your grandfather stopped believing long before he stopped belonging. I never worked out which one I inherited."

Aidan looked through the doorway at the low chairs, at Helen listening to an aunt, at the sheets over the mirrors where his grandfather used to check his cap before walking down to the water. His grandfather had been the one who said make it up as you go, and his grandfather had also been the one who sat through seven days of mourning when his own wife died, forty years ago, because that was what his mother had done. Both of those had been the same man. Aidan had spent years treating his grandfather's silence about religion as absence, and now he was sitting in a house full of evidence that it had been something else, though he couldn't say what, exactly.

"You belong out there more than I do," he said finally. "He'd want you in the chair."

"You don't know that."

"No," Aidan admitted. "I don't."

His mother dried the clean dish with a towel, folded it, put it down, picked it up again. Out in the living room, the uncles had started a different story, something about a dog and a rowboat, and Helen was laughing again without covering her mouth this time. His mother smoothed her skirt, the way he'd seen her do before walking into a meeting she'd rather skip, and went in and sat down in the empty low chair beside her aunt, who reached over without pausing her story and took her hand.

Aidan carried the jello salad out to the porch, where Mr. MacLeod from next door was leaning on the rail, looking at the lake. "He used to stand right there," Mr. MacLeod said, pointing at the end of the dock. "Every evening, like a sentry." Below them the water was flattening toward dark, and Aidan skipped the last flat stone from his pocket, once, twice, six times, before it went under.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal distance a projectile travels equals its constant horizontal velocity multiplied by its time in the air.
story:
The playground had emptied by late afternoon, leaving the swings to move faintly in the wind and a single basketball under the hoop near the fence. William sat on the top of the climbing structure with his physics workbook open on his knees, though he had stopped reading it ten minutes ago. Below him, Saad paced the rubberized ground with the basketball tucked under one arm, and Loan sat cross-legged at the base of the slide, timing nothing yet, her phone flat in her palm.

"Throw it," William called down. "From the free throw line, same throw every time."

Saad looked at him the way he looked at most of William's schemes, blase and slightly amused, as though the world had long since stopped surprising him. "You want me to stand here shooting hoops so you can pass physics."

"I want you to stand there shooting hoops so I can understand it. There's a difference."

Loan held up her phone. "I've got the stopwatch. Just tell me when."

The problem in the workbook was the one that had defeated him on Thursday night and again on Sunday. A ball launched at a known angle and speed, and the question asking where it would land. He could find how long it stayed in the air; the vertical part made sense to him, gravity pulling steadily downward, the numbers behaving. But the horizontal part felt like guesswork, and Mr. Cho had written a small red question mark beside his answer, which was wrong by eight meters. Eight meters was a lot. Eight meters was the difference between the ball landing on the court and landing in the flowerbed.

Saad shot. Loan tapped her phone, and when the ball bounced she stopped the timer and called out, "One point one seconds." William jogged to where it had struck, counted heel-to-toe paces back to the line, and wrote both numbers in the margin of his workbook. Then he stood very still, doing the arithmetic twice, because the result seemed too tidy.

"Four and a half meters," he said.

Saad retrieved the ball. "So?"

"Time was one point one seconds. Distance was four and a half meters. So it crossed about four meters every second, the whole way. The whole flight." He crouched and drew the numbers with his finger in the wood chips. "Nothing slows it sideways. It just goes at that speed the whole time it's up there."

Loan came over, shielding the phone screen from the low sun. "So if you know how fast it's going sideways, and you know how long it's in the air..."

"One multiplication. That's the landing spot." He said it quietly, almost beseeching the sentence to remain true under another test. "Do it again. Different throw, harder one."

They ran the drill five more times, Saad varying his shots with theatrical care, Loan calling out times like a race official, William pacing distances and scribbling. On the fourth throw he predicted the landing point before the ball arrived, standing with his heel planted where he believed it would strike, and it hit half a pace away, close enough that Saad accused him of witchcraft. On the fifth he was a full pace off, and he stood looking at the ball where it had actually landed, refusing to round the difference away.

"My fault," Loan offered. "I might have stopped late. My thumb slipped."

"Or my paces aren't honest. I take longer steps when I'm tired." He was honest about it in his notebook, too: wrote both numbers, then wrote that he could not yet tell which measurement had lied. Mr. Cho would want that, he suspected. Mr. Cho had a way of asking, in class, not what the answer was but which part of the answer you trusted least, and William had always found the question embarrassing until this moment, standing in a playground with a number that almost worked.

Saad lobbed the ball high and short, a lazy arc that hung against the paling sky. William timed it himself this time, counting in his head, and walked to where his method said it should come down. It landed just past his left shoe, kicking wood chips onto his sneaker.

"Now you're just showing off," Loan said, and Saad, already moving to pick up the ball again, called back, "Ask me something harder."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Benjamin Franklin had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed in London in 1769, using knowledge from his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain.
story:
Ethan spread the current map across the picnic table in his backyard, weighting the corners with his mother's gardening stones so the afternoon wind couldn't fold it back into its creases. The Atlantic was printed in bands of blue and orange, and along the eastern edge of North America a ribbon of red wound northeast like a vein. Somewhere in that ribbon was the answer to Ms. Wong's assignment: explain, in his own words, how warm water off Florida ends up keeping boreal cities like Oslo and Dublin from freezing as hard as they should at their latitude. He had until Monday. It was Saturday.

Joyce arrived first, carrying two binders and a laptop she never opened. She wanted an A on this presentation, and she said so within a minute of sitting down, because she had a scholarship interview in three weeks and she wanted to be able to say the word oceanography without feeling like a fraud. Nikita came through the gate with his shoes already untied, holding a printout he'd found at one in the morning. "Look at this," he said, laying it over Ethan's map. It was an old engraving, cruder than the satellite chart, the current drawn as a series of looping arrows. "That's from 1769. Benjamin Franklin had it printed in London."

Ethan leaned over it. The shape was the same shape, the same curve his modern map showed in color. "Wait, how," he said. "There were no satellites. There was barely anything."

"Ships," Nikita said. "Whalers." He tapped the caption. "Franklin's cousin. Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain."

Joyce frowned at the engraving. "So the captains already knew about the current before anyone printed it?"

"That's the part that's messing me up," Ethan said. He sat back on the bench and looked at the fence, at the neighbor's overgrown hydrangea, because it was easier to think looking at something that didn't matter. "Folger knew it from sailing it. Franklin put it on paper for people who'd never been on the water. Two completely different kinds of knowing, and the chart is where they meet." He heard himself sounding like a college brochure and stopped, but not before Joyce wrote something down.

She wrote fast, then argued with herself out loud, which was how she worked. "For the presentation I could do the science side. Heat transport, the westerlies, all the mechanisms. That's what gets graded. But the Franklin thing is a better story. Ship captains were saving days by avoiding the current, getting to London faster than the mail packets that kept sailing straight through it. That's a story people remember."

"Use both," Nikita said. He was lying on the grass now, holding the engraving above his face. "My dad says every good argument is two arguments wearing one coat."

Ethan laughed, then stopped, because it was actually true and he hadn't expected it from Nikita's dad. He pulled the modern map back toward him and traced the red ribbon with one finger, from Florida up past the Grand Banks and across toward Europe. His father's whole approach to problems was to find the expert and follow the expert, no questions. His mother's was to distrust every expert until she'd worked it out herself. He had spent seventeen years assuming he had to pick one. But here was Franklin taking Folger's knowledge, drawn from decades of deck time and whale oil and dead reckoning, and trusting it enough to print it for the world. Not blind trust. Not lonely doubt. Something in between, with a chart at the center.

"Here's what I still can't answer, though," he said. "Nobody in 1769 knew why the current carried heat north. Folger just knew what it did to a ship. So the whalers had the fact and not the reason, and we have the reason and maybe not the fact, not the way they had it." He shrugged. "I don't know what to do with that. I'll probably just say it out loud in the presentation and hope Ms. Wong doesn't mark me down for admitting a hole."

"She won't," Joyce said. "She's the one who put the Franklin engraving on the reading list in the first place. Page nine, footnote four. You're welcome." She began rearranging the stones on the map's corners, squaring them like she was setting a table. Nikita sat up and read the engraving's caption aloud again, slower this time, the way you read something you intend to keep. When they finally gathered their things, dusk had come on without any of them noticing, and the red ribbon of the Gulf Stream had gone grey in the fading light, still pointing northeast across the page. Ethan folded the map along its old creases and carried it inside under his arm.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Spike tape is coloured tape used to mark where furniture and actors should be placed on the stage floor.
story:
Brody pushed the living room furniture against the walls on Saturday morning, and by noon his mother's sofa had become the central prop of a one-act play. The drama teacher, Ms. Oyelaran, had given him the directing job with a warning attached to it, something about how directing was mostly listening and only partly deciding, and he was still turning that over in his mind the way he turned over a proof in math class, waiting for the structure to show itself. He had three weeks. He had two actors. He had a living room with a rug.

Rose arrived first, script rolled in her back pocket, and Yasmine came twenty minutes late carrying a bag of clementines and an apology she didn't seem to feel. The play was about two sisters clearing out their dead mother's apartment, which meant it needed a sofa, a lamp, and a lot of silence. Brody had spent two evenings deciding where the sofa should go. Upstage centre, he had written in his notebook, though his living room had no stage, only a rug whose fringe marked the edge of the imaginary world.

"Okay," he said. "Rose, you come in from the kitchen. Yasmine, you're already sitting. You don't look up."

Yasmine sat. She looked up immediately.

"You look up," Brody said.

"I'm a person, Brody. People look up when doors open."

He hadn't thought of it that way. In his head the movement had been a geometry problem, arrows on graph paper, each actor a point moving through space, and the arrows were supposed to mean something, tension or avoidance or grief. He sketched the scene twice more and both times something in it sagged. Rose hovered near the sofa arm. Yasmine drifted off it. Nobody stayed where he had put them.

They ran the scene a fourth time and he finally saw the actual problem, which was not the actors at all. The sofa moved. Every time Rose leaned against the arm, the whole thing skidded an inch across the hardwood, and Yasmine followed it like a moon, and by the end of the scene the sisters were having their most painful conversation in what was effectively the dining room. He measured with his eye where the sofa had started and where it had ended and felt a small, clean anger at himself for not noticing sooner.

"You need spike tape," Rose said, when he explained it. She said it the way other people said pencil or stapler.

"Spike tape?"

"Coloured tape. It marks where furniture and actors should be placed on the stage floor." She shrugged. "My cousin does tech. It's all they talk about."

The hardware store had nothing called that, but the cashier found him a roll of yellow floor tape, and on Sunday he tore off pieces and laid them at the sofa's feet, small yellow flags on the hardwood, and then, because the thought arrived and he liked it, two short strips for Yasmine's starting position and one for the door Rose entered through. He wondered whether this was what directing was, this translation of an idea into marks on a floor, a lemma laid down so that a larger truth could be proved on top of it. He didn't say that out loud. Yasmine had already told him he got garrulous when he was nervous, narrating his own decisions like a nature documentary, and she wasn't wrong.

The next rehearsal held. The sofa stayed put. And something unexpected came of the stillness: because Yasmine couldn't drift, she had to do something else with her restlessness, and what she did was pick up the clementine from the end table and peel it in one long spiral during Rose's monologue, not looking at her sister, the peel curling down past her knee. Rose stopped mid-line to watch. Then she finished the line differently, quieter, and the room changed around the two of them. Brody sat on the floor by the bookshelf with his notebook forgotten in his lap, enraptured, hardly breathing, trying to notice how it worked without breaking it by noticing.

He still didn't know whether he was a director or just a boy with tape. Ms. Oyelaran had said listen, and he had mostly decided, and the tape had been a decision, but the clementine had been Yasmine's, and the quiet had been Rose's, and maybe directing was the strange arithmetic of adding those things to what you'd already laid down on the floor. He could hold both ideas at once, he thought, the way the scene held both sisters. What he couldn't do was know whether the yellow strips would survive his mother, who would want her living room back by Friday.

At the end of the rehearsal Yasmine dropped the clementine peel, intact, a full spiral, onto the tape at her feet.

"Keep that," Rose said. "Mark it. New spike."

Brody tore off a piece of tape and put it beside the peel.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues' 1993 study of violinists described 'deliberate practice': effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours.
story:
Grayson set the last cone down on the worn patch of grass behind his aunt's house and counted the kids twice, because Milan always hid behind the shed when drills started. Nine of them, all eleven and twelve, all wearing the maroon shirts of a team nobody had bothered to teach anything. They had lost their last four games by a combined score he refused to say out loud, and in every one of those losses the same thing had happened: a pass rolled to nobody, a pass sailed out, a pass that should have been easy died at the receiver's feet.

"Scrimmage," said Milan, emerging from behind the shed as if summoned. The others echoed it, a low hopeful chant, and Grayson understood the pull. Scrimmage was fun. Scrimmage was the whole reason they'd signed up. He had scrimmaged his way through three years of this league himself, and it had never once made him better at anything.

"Not today," he said. "Today we pass."

Kellen dropped his backpack on the porch step and came down into the yard, still holding the printout Grayson had texted him at midnight. "You actually read this whole thing?"

"I read it twice." Grayson lined up the gates he'd made from two cones each, spaced across the grass like teeth. "These guys have played, what, two hundred hours of soccer? Two hundred hours and Danny still can't hit a teammate eight feet away. Hours aren't the thing."

"So what is the thing?"

"Ericsson and his colleagues did a study in 1993," Grayson said. "Violinists. The best ones hadn't just logged more hours. The practice that mattered was different." He handed Kellen the printout, which was covered in his own pencil marks, whole paragraphs crossed out and one sentence boxed three times. "It's called deliberate practice. Effortful work on a specific weakness, with immediate feedback. That's the whole difference."

Kellen scanned the boxed sentence. "You're being facetious with this pencil work, right? Nobody boxes a sentence three times."

"I boxed it three times so I wouldn't forget it."

"Okay, coach." Kellen folded the paper into his pocket. "But they're eleven. Effortful is not their brand."

They started simple. Two players, one gate, four yards apart, ten passes through the middle. Every pass that missed the gate meant the passer had to retrieve the ball himself and start his count over, which Danny found out immediately and loudly. Grayson stood where Danny could see him, and after each attempt he called the one thing that had gone wrong: hips closed, plant foot pointing at the fence, eyes up before the touch. Not encouragement, not a speech. One correction, immediately, the way the sentence in the box said.

The kids hated it for exactly eleven minutes. Grayson watched the hatred happen, minute by minute, the slumping shoulders and the appeals to Kellen, who had stationed himself by the water jug as a kind of appeals court. Then something shifted, and it shifted through Danny, of all people. Danny hit nine gates in a row, and Milan saw him do it, and the yard turned competitive in a way scrimmage had never made it, because in scrimmage you could hide and in this you couldn't. Grayson felt something loosen in his own chest, the specific relief of a plan meeting the world and surviving.

Kellen had been watching Danny from the jug, and he was the first to notice that Danny's misses had changed character. Earlier, the boy had been snatching at the ball, flinching into each pass as though it might bite him. Now the misses were long, relaxed, a touch too much weight on a ball struck with actual intention, and Kellen recognized the difference because his phonetics professor called it the same thing whether you were mapping vowel shifts or watching a kid learn a touch: an error made with control is a different animal from an error made without it. He had spent the semester thinking that class was useless. Standing in this yard, watching a twelve-year-old sculpt his own mistake into something readable, he revised the opinion.

"You made him quieter," Kellen said when Grayson came over for water. "You know that? Half your coaching is just shutting up in the right places."

"I'm copying," Grayson said. "The violin teachers in the study. They gave feedback right away, but the students did the work. I can't want it more than Danny does."

"Milan wants it more than Danny does."

"Milan wants the scrimmage."

Kellen looked at the gates, then at the kids, who had gone gray-faced and quiet with effort, Milan loudest among them, shouting his own count, and he thought about how the fun had come back anyway, but changed, attached to difficulty instead of hiding from it. He was aware of a small worry under the thought. The study had been about violinists, solitary and driven and grown, and this was a backyard full of children on a Saturday, and he didn't know if a thing that worked in a music practice room transferred all the way down to eleven-year-olds, or whether some of what they were doing was only theater with cones. Grayson didn't seem to share the worry. Grayson had boxed a sentence three times and trusted it.

"Two more minutes of gates," Grayson called out, "then we scrimmage."

The yard erupted, and beneath the cheering Danny jogged back to his station alone, set his ball down, and waited for Milan with his plant foot already turned toward the target.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: On Mexico's Day of the Dead, orange marigolds called cempasúchil decorate altars and graves, because their bright color and strong scent are thought to guide the souls of the dead home.
story:
The house smelled of tangerines and dust, the way it always had, except that the woman who had kept the tangerines in the blue bowl was not in the kitchen anymore. Maika stood in the doorway with her mother's list folded in her pocket, staring at the folding table her aunts had set up in the living room. On it they had arranged a photograph, a small glass of water, and a pile of pan dulce still in its paper bag, but the table looked bald to her, unfinished, and everyone kept glancing at the empty space at the center as if it were an accusation.

"The flowers," her mother said. "The market on Ninth Street. Ask for the man with the two awnings, he saves them for us every year." She pressed bills into Maika's hand, and her aunt followed her out onto the porch, still wiping her hands on a dish towel.

Tyrell was already sitting on the porch steps, because Tyrell was always somewhere nearby in November, claiming his grandmother had promised him tamales. He stood up when he saw Maika's face. "What kind of flowers?" he asked.

"Orange marigolds," the aunt said. "Cempasúchil. They have to be those." She said the word the way Maika's grandmother had said it, with the emphasis falling soft in the middle.

"Why those?" Tyrell asked. "The yellow ones are half the price."

"Because they go on the altar for Day of the Dead," the aunt said, already turning back inside. "Their color and their scent are supposed to guide the souls home." She let the screen door bang behind her, which in that house meant the conversation was over, though nothing had really been explained.

The market was fourteen blocks away, and by the time they reached it Maika's dress shoes had burned two blisters into her heels. The man with the two awnings shook his head over his crates. He had marigolds, but the frost had come early and the frost had turned them pale, a jaundiced yellow that nobody wanted for an altar. "Try the back," he said. "The woman with the red truck." The woman with the red truck had sold out by ten in the morning. Two more stalls, two more shaking heads, and Tyrell counting the remaining bills with the expression of someone watching a plan disintegrate. "We could just get the yellow ones," he said. "She'd understand, right?"

Maika looked down the aisle of the market, past the baskets of chiles and the stacked sugar skulls with their empty grins, and thought about her grandmother, who had been exact about everything: about the blue bowl, about the genealogy recited every Christmas back to a town in Jalisco nobody else had seen, about which grandchild was allowed to touch the radio. She had not been sentimental. She had simply believed that certain things were done a certain way, and Maika understood suddenly that this was why the aunts kept glancing at the empty center of the table. It was not decoration they were missing. It was a set of directions.

"There's the garden center," she said. "Past the tracks. Seedlings, cuttings, whatever they have." They walked another twenty minutes while the afternoon burnished itself into gold behind the water tower, and Maika spent the bus money on two flats of the brightest orange marigolds the greenhouse had, with a scent so strong it followed them down the block like a dog. She carried the flats the whole way back with the soil warming her forearms, and Tyrell carried the second flat and did not complain, which for Tyrell was a kind of eulogy.

The porch light was on when they turned the corner. Her mother came out, took one look at the flats, and laughed, a sound so unexpected that Maika stopped on the walk. "Come see," her mother said, and led them around the side of the house, past the lime tree, to the strip of garden along the back fence where no one had planted anything in years. The last of the daylight was on a whole row of marigolds, orange and enormous and drenched in that same heavy scent, gone to seed and gone wild since September, waiting along the fence where her grandmother had put them in the ground one spring and never said a word about it.

Maika stood there holding her flats from the market, blisters aching, money gone, and behind her the screen door opened and her aunt called out, "Set them by the table anyway. She always said you can't have too many."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: A lease that says 'utilities included' may cover only some utilities; the lease wording decides which, so each utility has to be checked separately.
story:
Charlie spread the two leases across the laminated table in the driving school's waiting room, weighting the corners with her keys and a vending machine soda she had no intention of drinking. Outside the window, an instructor was guiding a white sedan through orange cones with the patience of someone who had done this ten thousand times. Charlie had her own lesson in half an hour, but her mother had handed her the leases that morning at the bus stop, both of them printed off in the school library, and said, "You're better with numbers than I am. Tell me which one we can afford." Her mother worked nights at the hospital and slept through most of the daylight, so the decision had landed on Charlie, sixteen or not.

The first apartment, on Cleary Street, advertised utilities included, five hundred and sixty a month cheaper than the second. Charlie had nearly circled it in pencil before she made herself slow down. Cheap had a smell to it, the way a car that started too easily on a cold morning did. She thought of her father, two apartments and three years ago, signing a lease in the kitchen of the old place while she did homework at the same table. He had not read past the first page. "It says included," he had said to her mother, tapping the paper like a judge closing a case, and then the first electric bill had arrived in October and the two of them had sat with it between them, not touching it, the way people sit with a letter they already know is bad.

The pencil hovering over Cleary Street, she found the section headed Additional Provisions and read it with the care her driving instructor, Ms. Abdi, was always asking of her at intersections. The lease said the landlord included water, sewer, and trash collection. That was all it said. There was no mention of electricity anywhere, no mention of gas or internet, and when she flipped to the definition of "utilities" buried in clause fourteen, it listed exactly the same three. Something in her chest settled, unpleasantly, like the moment in the car when you realize the lane you chose is ending.

"So?" Kiara slid into the chair across from her, still in her work uniform from the bakery, smelling faintly of cinnamon. Kiara was the one everyone at school wanted to lionize whenever she aced something, teachers holding up her essays as though she were a prodigy and not just someone who read carefully, and Charlie sometimes thought Kiara hated it more than she let on.

"Utilities included doesn't mean all utilities," Charlie said. She turned the lease around so Kiara could see. "This one includes water and trash and nothing else. Electricity is separate. So it's only cheaper if electricity costs nothing, and electricity never costs nothing." She pulled out her phone and opened the calculator app, then closed it, then opened it again. "My dad found this out the hard way. We had to put space heaters on a payment plan one winter."

Kiara leaned in and read clause fourteen twice, the way she read everything. "The other one's worse, then?"

"Maybe not." Charlie flattened the second lease, the one on Halden Road, which cost more but stated plainly in its own fine print that water, sewer, trash, and heat were included, heat being gas, and electricity was billed to the tenant at a fixed flat rate written into the lease itself, forty dollars a month. She did the arithmetic twice because she did not trust herself the first time: Halden's rent plus the forty, against Cleary's rent plus an electricity bill she could only guess at. She had her mother's old bills from the last apartment in her backpack, filed in a folder she had started keeping the way other people kept ticket stubs.

The door to the back hallway opened and Ms. Abdi came out with a clipboard, her nemesis when it came to Charlie's parallel parking, though Charlie privately thought of her more as an ally who happened to hold a clipboard. Ms. Abdi glanced at the papers on the table without slowing, then slowed anyway. "Homework in my waiting room," she said. "Ambitious."

"Sort of," Charlie said. "We might move. I'm figuring out which lease is actually cheaper, and one of them only looks cheaper because of what included means."

Ms. Abdi nodded once and did not offer anything further, which was one of the things Charlie liked about her, and tapped the clipboard. "Five minutes, Charlie. Cone course."

Kiara had taken over the calculator, checking Charlie's totals line by line, and when she finished she looked up. "Halden's about thirty a month more than Cleary, if Cleary's electric bill is around what your mom paid before. If it's more than that, Halden wins. But you can't actually know Cleary's bill from here."

"That's the part I hate," Charlie said. She wrote both numbers on a napkin, drew a box around the unknown, and texted her mother a photo of clause fourteen with the message: "Can you ask Cleary's landlord for an average electric bill for that unit?" The reply would take hours, since her mother was asleep behind a blackout curtain across town. Charlie gathered the leases into the folder, squared them against the table edge, and stood. Halden was probably the one, but probably was a word with soft edges, and she would not sign anything her mother had not held in her own hands.

She pushed through the door to the lot, where Ms. Abdi stood beside the white sedan, cones laid out in their patient rows, and the morning traffic on the avenue behind them went quietly on.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Simple interest is calculated as I = P times r times t: the principal, times the annual interest rate, times the time in years.
story:
I am, by my own account, the most financially sensible person I know, which is why I found myself in the queue at the bank on a Tuesday in June, holding a withdrawal slip for money I did not yet have. The plan was flawless in the way that only my plans are: borrow three hundred dollars from my uncle, fix the Camry's alternator, start the delivery job on Monday, and pay everything back before summer ended. Esme had come along because she claimed the bank had air conditioning and her house did not, and because she did not believe a word I said about being sensible, though she was polite enough not to say so except constantly.

The trouble had begun two nights earlier, in my uncle's kitchen, over his turbid glass of iced tea that he never stirred and always finished. He said he'd lend me the three hundred, but he wanted it to be, in his word, real. "Six percent," he said. "Simple interest, one year. You want to act like a businessman, I'll treat you like one." I agreed on the spot, because agreeing quickly is one of my gifts, and I told him I'd have the paperwork sorted by Wednesday. I did not mention that I had no idea what simple interest amounted to, because I also have my pride, which I keep in better repair than the Camry.

At the bank I filled out the slip, then un-filled it, then filled it out again for a smaller amount, a man improvising with great deliberateness. Esme watched from the plastic chairs by the window. "You're sweating," she observed. "Banks are cold. It's uncanny."

"It's the responsibility," I said. "It weighs on people like me."

Behind the counter, Ms. Boateng, who had been my economics teacher two years ago and now, apparently, worked here on summer Tuesdays, waved me over. I hadn't known she had a second life. This unsettled me more than the loan. Teachers, I had always predicate​d my entire schooling on the assumption that they simply stopped existing at 3:15, dissolved back into whatever staff room they came from.

"Raphael," she said. "You look like a man about to sign something."

"I'm borrowing from family," I said, with dignity. "Three hundred, six percent, simple, one year."

"And do you know what that costs you?"

I said, with the confidence of a person who had, that morning, read half a pamphlet in the lobby, "Simple interest is the principal times the rate times the time." It came out flat, like a line memorized from the pamphlet, which it was, though I'd pieced together what it meant on the drive over, doing arithmetic with my thumb on the steering wheel at red lights. Principal three hundred, rate point-oh-six, time one. Eighteen dollars. I told her the number. She checked it, in her head, faster than I liked.

"Eighteen," she confirmed. "Not nothing, not fatal." She slid a pamphlet across the counter, the same one I'd read, and then, because the queue behind me was short, she asked what I was doing with the money on the other side. I explained the alternator, the delivery job, the flawless plan. She asked whether I had anything in savings. I said yes, technically, a junior account my grandmother opened when I was nine, forty dollars of birthday money I'd been guarding like a dragon.

She typed. She turned the monitor toward me. The forty dollars had become forty-one sixty. "It compounds," she said, and left it there, moving on to the next customer, which I considered dereliction of her teaching duty, though technically she was off duty.

Esme came up beside me and read the screen. "Your money made a dollar sixty doing nothing," she said. "While you were making plans."

"It's not the same thing," I said. "A dollar sixty and eighteen dollars are different magnitudes."

"They're the same direction," she said. "That's the whole thing. Interest is interest. You're paying it on one side and collecting it on the other, and you never once thought about the second side until a woman in a vest showed you a screen."

I wanted to argue, and I assembled several arguments, all of them sound, all of them mine. But I kept looking at the forty-one sixty. My uncle's eighteen dollars suddenly seemed less like a toll and more like tuition, and I couldn't decide whether that made the loan smarter or me stupider, or whether those were even different categories. Perhaps, I thought, the artifice of my own competence had been the most expensive thing I owned, and it had cost me nothing so far only because no one had ever audited it.

I signed the withdrawal slip, took the three hundred, and walked out with Esme into the heat. My phone buzzed. It was my uncle: "Scratch the six percent. Your grandmother called me. She says charge you nothing and you'll learn nothing. So: seven."

I stood in the parking lot doing the new arithmetic with my thumb, twenty-one dollars, twenty-one, and heard Esme laughing before I'd said a word.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In The Catcher in the Rye, published in 1951, the narrator Holden Caulfield tells readers, 'I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life.'
story:
The bus smelled of diesel and rain-soaked jackets, and Alyssa had the essay prompt folded into her pocket like a confession she hadn't read yet. Mr. Tan had written it on the board an hour before: "Can we trust a narrator who tells us he lies? Discuss with reference to The Catcher in the Rye." Due Monday. She dropped into the seat across from Daniyal, who was already halfway through a bag of chips he'd hidden inside his sleeve like contraband.

"Okay, hot take," she said, pulling the book from her bag. "Holden's a liar. He says so, like, right away. Chapter three." She flipped to the page, the spine cracking the way a spine does when a book has been read by four seniors before you. She read it out loud over the engine noise: "'I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life.'" She looked up. "Published in 1951, this book. Seventy-some years of students, and every single one of us falls for him anyway."

Daniyal crunched thoughtfully. "So he's lying about lying, which means he's telling the truth, which means he's lying. My brain just did a cartwheel." He offered her a chip, which was his version of a peace treaty. "Maybe that's your essay. He can't lie about lying without telling the truth. It's a paradox, like the barber who shaves everyone who doesn't shave themselves."

"That's not it, though," Alyssa said, and heard herself say it before she fully knew why. "He's not doing logic puzzles. He's warning us. Like a disclaimer." She turned the book over in her hands. "Think about who tells you up front that they can't be trusted. Nobody. Con artists don't announce it. So why does he?"

Elianne boarded at the second stop, hair dripping, and wedged in beside Daniyal without asking, which was the arrangement they'd had since ninth grade. "What are we arguing about?" she said, and when Alyssa showed her the line, Elianne studied it the way she studied everything, with her chin tucked like she was checking it for counterfeit bills. "Maybe he lies about the little stuff," Elianne said slowly. "The boring stuff. How many taxis, what he ordered for lunch. So we believe him about the big stuff. He says he's a liar, and then he tells us Allie died, and we believe the second thing because he paid for it with the first."

The bus lurched around the corner by the Dollar Store and everyone's backpacks slid like a landslide. Alyssa held the book steady. That was the thing, she realized; the admission didn't circumscribe what you believed, it widened it. By confessing to the small lies, Holden bought credit for the large truths, and the reader handed it over without counting it. She'd been doing it all week herself, she thought with a small cold drop of honesty. Her mother had asked about the college applications and Alyssa had said "almost done," which was a lie, so that "I'm fine, honestly" would land like truth. It hadn't worked, or maybe it had, which was worse.

"Wait," Daniyal said, sitting up so fast a chip flew into the aisle. "The etymology thing. You told me about this last week, that 'sincere' might come from 'without wax.' Sculptors who covered cracks in marble with wax, and honest ones sold their stuff sine cera. If that's true, then a sincere narrator is one who shows you the cracks." He grinned. "Holden's showing us the cracks on purpose. He's a sincere liar. I want that on a shirt."

"Etymology is mostly folk myth, Daniyal, that one's probably fake," Elianne said, but she was smiling, and Alyssa wrote it in her notebook anyway, because a useful lie and a useful truth looked identical at this distance. She wrote other things too, fast, while the bus rattled past the car wash and the shuttered video store: the small lies are load-bearing; the confession is a strategy; the question isn't whether he lies but which lies we need him to tell. She couldn't decide, though, and the not-deciding bothered her like a pebble in a shoe. Maybe Elianne was right and the confessions were currency. Maybe he was lying about Allie too, about the whole friable shape of his grief, and she'd built sympathy on nothing. The page didn't settle it. She underlined "terrific" three times and stared at it.

They pulled up at the loop and the doors gasped open. Rain came in sideways under the awning, and everyone crowded toward the front, jackets up. Daniyal held the chip bag over Elianne's head like an umbrella, which protected approximately nothing. Alyssa stepped down last, the essay prompt still folded in her pocket, softer now from handling. She thought she had half an answer, the half where lying out loud makes a narrator believable, and she was honest enough to admit the other half, the part where she might be getting played by a fictional boy from 1951, was still open. "Text me if you figure out the sincere liar shirt," Elianne called from under the ruined chip bag, and Alyssa laughed and raised the novel above her head against the rain.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Any member of the US House of Representatives may introduce a bill in the House, and it is then referred to a committee for study.
story:
The folding chairs had been arranged in rows that almost faced the podium, and by seven minutes past seven most of them were full, which surprised Alexandra, who had expected a dozen retirees and a reporter. The town hall had been called about the Route 9 crossing, where her brother had been clipped by a truck in March, and where, in the eleven years before that, three other people had been hit, one of them a paper carrier on a bicycle. Alexandra had spent two weeks after the accident reading the website of the United States House of Representatives until nearly midnight, making notes in the margin of her chemistry homework, and she had sent an email to the office of their congressman asking whether he would introduce a law requiring a pedestrian signal at crossings like that one. The reply had arrived four days later, brief and almost polite, from a staffer named only in the signature block, saying that the congressman appreciated her concern.

Mr. Weiss sat two rows ahead of her, alone, his coat folded across his knees with a care that suggested he did not intend to leave early. He had taught English at the high school until her sophomore year, and she had taken his elective on hermeneutics, the close reading of difficult texts, where he had made them spend three weeks on a single page of Melville. He was famously reticent at neighborhood gatherings, answering questions about himself with a redirect toward the questioner, and she had never once seen him at a public meeting. She caught herself watching the back of his head instead of the moderator.

The moderator opened the floor, and a man in a county windbreaker stood to expostulate about budgets, his voice climbing until the microphone crackled. A woman from the cycling club countered with a petition, and Nicholas, who had ridden to the meeting with Alexandra, leaned over and whispered that half these people just liked the sound of their own names in the minutes. She told him to hush. Then a young woman in a blazer introduced herself as a field representative from the congressman's office, in town to hear residents, and Alexandra's stomach dropped because that was the office, that was the signature block.

When the representative asked if anyone had a concrete proposal, Alexandra raised her hand before she could reconsider. She stood, holding her notes, and said that she had emailed the office in April. "I found out that any member of the House of Representatives can introduce a bill," she said, "and then it gets referred to a committee for study. So I asked him to introduce one. For the crossing." The room turned toward her, and the field representative's face changed into something careful and attentive, the way a receptionist looks up a name she has been told to watch for. "You're Alexandra," the woman said. "Your email's in the file. I printed it out."

I had not expected the file to be real. I had imagined my words dissolving somewhere in a server in Washington, and hearing that a person had printed them, had carried them into this room with the folding chairs, made my mouth go dry. The woman explained what would happen if the congressman agreed: the bill would be introduced, studied in committee, debated, voted on, and, if it survived the Senate too, signed or not signed by the president. She said it plainly, without promising anything, and I respected that more than the man in the windbreaker's promises about money that did not exist.

"Say he introduces it," Nicholas called out from beside me. "How long?" The woman said she couldn't say, and a man near the back said that was the whole problem with Washington, and the moderator tapped the podium for order.

It was then that Mr. Weiss stood. He did not go to the microphone at first; he spoke from his row, so that everyone had to lean toward him, and his voice was quieter than anyone expected. He said that he had driven that stretch of Route 9 twice a day for nineteen years. He said that in March he had been the truck. The crossing had been empty, he said, and then it had not been, and the boy had come off the hood and stood up, which Mr. Weiss said he still did not understand, the standing up. He had wanted to come to the hospital, and had been told, kindly, by the boy's father, that it would be easier for everyone if he did not.

I looked at Nicholas and saw that he already knew. I had spent the spring telling anyone who would listen that the town needed to act, that the state needed to act, and the driver had been sitting in a folding chair the whole time, waiting for a meeting about the thing he had done. He said he did not ask anyone to forgive him, and that he did not know whether he deserved the crossing to be named in anybody's memory, but that he thought the bill should be introduced anyway, and studied, and argued over, and voted on, whatever the vote turned out to be. "I don't know if it would have helped," he said. "I've read the proposal twice. That's my whole statement."

The field representative wrote something in the margin of my printed email, and when the moderator asked whether anyone else wished to speak, no one did, exactly. The meeting did not end so much as thin out, people gathering coats and murmuring. She found me by the door. "He'll want to meet you," she said. "Thursday, if you can come to the district office." Nicholas asked whether I was going to say yes, and I said I didn't know yet, and I watched Mr. Weiss fold his chair back against the wall before he left.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A subgroup inside a poll has a larger margin of error than the whole poll: 200 people out of a 1,000-person sample carry a margin of about plus or minus 7 points.
story:
Julia had the poll open in one tab and her draft in the other, and for ten minutes she had been typing a headline and deleting it. "Young Voters Break Left on Housing, Poll Finds." She liked the shape of it. It was the kind of thing her editor at the town's online news site would put in big letters, the kind of thing that got shared.

She called Reilly first, because Reilly answered the way she always did, without saying hello, just "What."

"The poll Mr. Hoffmann sent us. Did you look at the crosstabs?"

"Honestly I looked at the top-line and closed it. Why, did you find something?"

"Sort of. I found a headline." Julia read it to her and heard Reilly's keyboard stop.

"Where's that number coming from?" Reilly asked.

"The 18-to-24 thing? It's in there. They asked a thousand people, and of those, about two hundred were in our age group, and it says something like 58 percent of us support the rent cap." Julia scrolled as she talked. The afternoon had gone torpid around her, the fan pushing warm air in circles, her cat asleep on the windowsill, but now she was wide awake.

"Two hundred out of a thousand. So it's one in five of the sample."

"Right." Julia clicked through to the methodology page, the part she usually skipped, the dense paragraph at the bottom that read like the terms of a loan agreement. She had sat through a unit on how banks amortize a mortgage over thirty years in Mr. Hoffmann's class, and this paragraph had the same feel, small print meant to be skimmed past. Except the small print was where the numbers lived, so she read it. Overall results carried a margin of error of about plus or minus 3 points. And then a line she had to read twice: figures for subgroups, such as age categories, have larger margins of error.

"How much larger?" Reilly asked when Julia read it aloud.

"It doesn't say for each one. Hang on." Julia opened a new tab and searched, half expecting to have to amortize her whole evening to this. The first result was a page about how polls actually worked. She skimmed past the general parts, the parts about random sampling, and found an example that stopped her: 200 people drawn from a 1,000-person sample carry a margin of error of about plus or minus 7 points.

"Seven," she said. "Plus or minus seven, for a group our size."

"So 58 percent could really be?"

"Could be 51. Could be 65. Or anything between." Julia sat back. On the screen her draft still glowed, the headline sitting there like it had been waiting to be caught. Fifty-one wasn't a majority of much; it was barely a leaning. Sixty-five was a landslide of opinion. The same number, depending on which side of the seven you landed. She thought about how strange that was, that the whole poll could say one thing confidently and its pieces could barely speak at all.

She called Noor next, because Noor was the one who argued for publishing anyway. "It's still interesting," Noor said. "It's a real pattern, two hundred people isn't nobody. And you can say the margin's bigger, somewhere in the story."

"In paragraph nine, where nobody reads."

"That's not my problem, that's the reader's problem."

"Then what's the headline?"

Noor paused, and Julia could hear her shrug through the phone, a little mannerism of hers, the pause before conceding nothing. "Young Voters Lean Left on Housing, Poll Suggests."

Julia typed it out. Lean. Suggests. The words were weaker and somehow more honest, and she understood that the weakness was the point, that a headline was a promise about how much you knew. She sat with both versions side by side in the document. The first one would travel farther. The second one told the truth about the size of her knowledge, which was: two hundred voices, speaking through a fog seven points wide.

Mr. Hoffmann had told them once, in the passing way he said the things that turned out to matter, that statistics was mostly the study of humility with numbers attached. She had written it down and forgotten it; now she felt it, the specific discomfort of wanting a clean story and having a blurry one instead.

She was still wondering whether blurriness could be made interesting, whether uncertainty itself could be the story, when she deleted the first headline, pasted the second, and hit send.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, a new employee fills out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.
story:
The application had been one page, but the folder Ms. Traoré handed her across the customer service desk was heavier than that, and Audrey carried it to the bench by the automatic doors like something she might spill. She was eighteen as of March, and this morning she had signed her name to a tax form for the first time in her life, at the grocery store where she'd been buying licorice since she was nine. The automatic doors kept opening for no one, letting in the heat, then sighing shut.

"You can fill that out here or take it home," Ms. Traoré had said, already turning back to the register. "Bring it back before your first shift Saturday."

The form itself was the problem. At the top it said Employee's Withholding Certificate, and beneath that, in smaller letters, Form W-4. She had assumed a first job meant a name tag and a register code, maybe a paper hat. Instead there were steps, like a math problem, and boxes for allowances that her father had once pontificated about at a barbecue, at length, until her uncle told him to let people eat. She had not listened. She wished, now, that she had listened.

She texted her mother: at the grocery store, got the job, but they gave me a form and I don't know what to put. She took a photo of the top of it and sent that too. Around her, carts rattled over the threshold of the doors; a cashier called for a price check on melons; somewhere in the back a machine hummed like it was thinking.

Her mother replied four minutes later, which for her mother was practically instant. It's called a W-4, she wrote. Your employer uses it to know how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. Then: Do you still have that green pen from Grandma? Audrey laughed out loud, alone on the bench, and a man with a case of soda glanced at her. Withhold. So some of her money would leave before it ever reached her. That felt like a thing she should have known, the way she should have known how to jump a car battery. She wondered what else was like this, invisible machinery under ordinary surfaces, waiting until you turned eighteen.

Kalli had told her last week that jobs were simple. You show up, you get paid, she'd said, dunking a fry in ketchup. But Kalli had never had a job either, and Audrey was beginning to suspect that Kalli's confidence was mostly an embryonic kind of certainty, something that hadn't yet met the world and been asked to fill out paperwork. There was a difference, Audrey thought, between knowing a thing and having proved it, the way in math class a lemma sat underneath the theorem, quietly doing the real work while the theorem got the name. The W-4 felt like that. Nobody put it on posters. It just sat under every paycheck in the country.

She filled in her name, her address, her Social Security number copied carefully from the card her mother had made her carry in a zipped pocket. At Step 2 she stopped again. There was something about other jobs, and she had no other jobs, so maybe she skipped it. Skipping felt like guessing, and guessing felt wrong on an official form, though she couldn't have said who would ever know. She texted her mother once more: what if I get it wrong? Her mother wrote back: people get them wrong all the time and fix them later. It's not a test. Audrey read that twice. Not a test. She had been treating it like one, holding her breath as if a wrong box meant failure instead of just a correction, a small lesson.

Gianluca came through the doors with a basket and spotted her before she could look casual. "You got it?" he said. "The job?" He had applied too, back in June, and hadn't heard anything, and there was a carefulness in how he asked, a hope he was keeping at a distance.

"I got it," she said. "But they gave me this." She held up the form so he could see the boxes, the steps, the blank lines.

Gianluca set his basket on the bench and took the form from her gently, like it might mean something for him too. "My cousin said you just put one and zero," he said. "Or zero and one. I can never remember which." He squinted at Step 3. "Why is it asking about kids? I don't have kids."

"Neither do I," Audrey said. "I think that part's not for us." She took the form back and looked at the lines she'd filled and the lines she hadn't. Somewhere in the store a register chimed, and Ms. Traoré's voice carried over the aisles, patient, telling someone where the olive oil was. Audrey wondered how many W-4s Ms. Traoré had watched get filled out at that bench, how many people had sat exactly there, pen hovering, not knowing what withholding meant.

She signed the last page with the pen her mother had given her, the green one, though she suspected it made no difference, and then sat with it a moment longer, reading over the steps she'd skipped. Gianluca watched her. "So how much do they take out?" he asked.

"I don't know yet," she said. "I guess I'll find out Saturday." She stood, squared the pages against her knee, and walked toward the customer service desk, where Ms. Traoré was waiting with her hand already out.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A deductive argument is called sound only when it is valid and all of its premises are actually true, so a sound argument's conclusion must be true.
story:
The seminar room smelled of whiteboard marker and the radiator's dusty heat, and Liam had claimed the seat by the window because it let him watch the flagpole rope knock against the metal in the wind when the discussion stalled. It stalled often. Twelve of them sat in a ring of pushed-together tables for the Friday elective Mr. Sato called Reasoning and Argument, and today the topic on the board read, in Mr. Sato's narrow capitals: IF EVERYONE JUMPED OFF A BRIDGE, WOULD YOU?

Liam had prepared nothing, which was unusual, because he had a real problem he wanted solved. In two weeks he was debating Memphis in the school finals, and Memphis had not lost all year. Liam had watched the video of her semifinal three times on his phone, late at night with one earbud in, pausing whenever she smiled at the judges before landing a point. Her arguments had a shape, that was the thing. They moved in lockstep, each step unavoidable, and by the end her conclusion looked like it had always been true, sitting there waiting to be noticed. He could feel himself being carried along even when he suspected she was wrong, and he could not locate where the carrying happened.

Marc-Andre, who sat opposite Liam and chewed his pen cap when he was thinking, was mid-argument about the bridge question. "Okay, say everyone actually is jumping. Then jumping is obviously rational, because everyone else has information you don't. The crowd can't all be wrong."

"The crowd can be wrong about basically everything," Memphis said. She was in this seminar too, of course she was, folding her hands on the table. "But that's not the point. The point is the form. If the bridge is on fire, and everyone who jumps survives, then anyone who jumps survives. So you should jump." She wrote it on the margin of her notebook, three neat lines, and turned it so the ring could see. "That argument is airtight. There's no hole in it."

Mr. Sato said nothing, only uncapped the marker and stood by the board, which was his way of handing the room to them.

Liam leaned forward. Something had snagged, the way a sleeve catches on a nail, small but stopping. "Airtight how?" he asked. His voice came out flatter than he meant, and Marc-Andre glanced at him. "I mean the structure. If those two things at the start are true, the end has to be true. I can't find a crack in the move from fire to survival to jumping. But." He stopped, and the radiator ticked, and out the window the flagpole rope clanked twice. "But the bridge isn't on fire. You just made that up to get the form you wanted."

"It's hypothetical," Memphis said, with the patience of someone explaining doors to a child. "That's the whole exercise."
