"I know it's hypothetical. I'm saying that's the difference." He took her notebook, asking with his eyebrows first, and read the three lines again. "The shape is perfect. If the premises are true the conclusion can't be false, no way around it. But the second premise is just, everyone who jumps survives. In the real one, the actual bridge, that's false. People drown." He looked up. "So what do we call it when the shape is right but a premise is wrong? Because it needs a name. Otherwise we'll keep calling it airtight and half the time we'll mean the shape and half the time we'll mean the whole thing."

Memphis was quiet for a second, and he watched her not blink. "Sound," she said finally. "An argument like that is only sound when it's valid and all of its premises are actually true. So a sound argument's conclusion must be true. Mine's valid. It isn't sound." She took the notebook back and looked at her three neat lines the way you look at a receipt for something you no longer own. "I've been calling those the same thing all season."

The word sat in the room. Marc-Andre pulled the pen cap from his mouth and said, mostly to the ceiling, "So the judges have been scoring us on shape this whole time," and Mr. Sato wrote SOUND on the board and underlined it twice, then drew an arrow from it to the word VALID and left a gap where the truth of premises would go, unlabelled, for them to fill.

Liam felt the snag loosen into something else, not triumph, closer to vertigo. He had what he needed for the finals: Memphis's arguments were beautiful machines that ran on premises nobody checked, and now he knew to check them. But the same blade cut his own side. His best case, the one about municipal water funding he'd rehearsed in the shower until the tiles memorized it, rested on a statistic from a single study he'd never traced to its source. He heard his own opening line in his head, insouciant, confident, and behind it now a small voice asking whether it was sound or merely valid, and he could not yet answer. It was also possible, he admitted to the table when they asked what he was staring at, that an argument with true premises and a mushy shape could still be right, that truth leaked in through doors form didn't guard, though Memphis said that way lay the autocrat's reasoning, decide the conclusion first and pick whatever carries you there.

"If you two are going to fight about it," Mr. Sato said, capping the marker, "fight about it in two weeks with timers on. Out. Enjoy the sun, it desensitizes you to how little summer you have left."

In the hallway Liam caught up with Memphis at the trophy case, where her name was already engraved on last year's plaque. "So in the finals," he said, "I'm going to say your premises are false. Out loud. Every time."

"I know," she said. "I'd think less of you if you didn't." She adjusted the strap of her bag and looked at the plaque, at her own name, and then at him. "Find your weakest premise before I do."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The 26th Amendment, which set the US voting age at 18, was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment.
story:
Riley's eighteenth birthday had fallen on a Tuesday, three weeks before the mayoral primary, which meant that for the first time in his life a sample ballot addressed to him was sitting on the kitchen table instead of in his mother's name. He carried it upstairs, set it beside his laptop, and opened the county election site, where a form asked him to declare a party. He had assumed that part would be easy.

It was not easy. The two candidates had spent the spring competing to dichotomize the town, the incumbent casting the challenger as a bulldozer who would pave the watershed, the challenger casting the incumbent as a man who had let the roads crumble while commissioning studies. Riley filled in the incumbent's circle on the sample ballot with a pencil, then erased it, and the smudge looked, in the lamp light, like a small gray country with disputed borders.

At dinner he brought the ballot downstairs and spread it beside the mashed potatoes. His grandfather, visiting for the week, put on his glasses and leaned over it. "First vote," he said. "You know I couldn't do that at your age."

"You weren't a citizen?"

"I was a citizen, I was drafted, I was eighteen, and I couldn't vote. None of us could. They changed it just before my birthday, actually. Nixon signed it, and before that summer was over it was law."

"That's fast," Riley said, genuinely startled, because amendments to him were museum objects, things ratified across decades of compromise.

"Faster than any of them, I heard. Some fella on a history program said the whole thing took about three months." His grandfather tapped the ballot. "So when people tell you it doesn't matter, you can tell them a whole country once decided it mattered enough to hurry."

Upstairs again, Riley opened a new tab and checked, because his grandfather also believed the moon landing had been staged "probably" and he had learned to verify. It checked out: the Twenty-sixth Amendment, setting the voting age at eighteen, ratified in 1971, about three months from start to finish, faster than any other amendment. He sat with that for a moment. Something had moved that quickly only because enough people had decided it was unbearable the other way, and one of those people, presumably, had been his grandfather, too young to matter and old enough to be drafted.

He texted Laiba, who had turned eighteen in October and had already voted in one school board election with the confidence of a person who had read every candidate's entire website. She called him within a minute.

"You're overthinking it," she said. "It's a primary."

"It's the first one. I want the reasoning to be sound, not just the feeling."

"There it is," Laiba said. "You and your logos. Everything has to be an argument with premises."

"Not everything. Just this." He told her about the amendment, the three months, the speed of it, and she was quiet in the way she was when something landed. "See, that's the part that gets me. They didn't vote for a candidate. They voted to make the voting itself possible. And now I'm sitting here erasing pencil marks."

"Then pick the one whose argument survives your worst mood," she said. "Not your best one. Your worst."

He hung up and opened the challenger's traffic plan, then the incumbent's watershed record, and took notes in the notebook he otherwise used for biology, where the top page still said phenotypic variation in the fast plants, Ms. Mokoena's block capitals from lab period. He laughed at himself briefly for applying lab rigor to a municipal primary, and then did it anyway, because the alternative was choosing on lawn signs.

At school the next day he cornered Coraly by the lockers, since she had actually attended a council meeting once for civics class. "The incumbent talks like a lawyer," she said. "The challenger talks like a coach. My mom says the coach type wins in years when people are tired of lawyers, which sounds cynical, but honestly watch the debate and tell me I'm wrong." He watched it that night, at the same desk, the laptop screen making a pale rectangle on the wall, and found that both of them dodged the one question he cared about, which was whether the new development off Route 9 would be approved. He understood then that his considered position was partly a guess, and that being honest about that was its own kind of reasoning, the kind his grandfather had never been permitted to need.

On the Saturday of the primary he walked to the middle school gym with his grandfather, who insisted on coming despite the knee. The line was short at nine in the morning. At the check-in table a volunteer asked Riley his name, found him in the binder, and handed him a slip.

"First time?" the volunteer said, already reaching for the small sticker that said I VOTED.

"First time," Riley said. He took the sticker and pressed it onto his grandfather's jacket instead, over the pocket, where it sat crooked and bright.

"I can't wear that," his grandfather said. "I'll get arrested."

"You won't get arrested."

"Somebody will say something. Millie Kowalski is over there by the pastries."

"Then let Millie Kowalski say something," Riley said, and got in line for the booth.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, but a methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average, much less time than carbon dioxide.
story:
The summer before college, Eli was supposed to be packing, but instead he was at his grandfather's house with a workbook from Ms. Nwosu's earth science class, the one course he'd taken seriously enough to finish early. He sat at the kitchen table under the window where the light came through the lace curtain and fell in small squares across a graph of carbon dioxide measured over the last hundred years, the line climbing in a slow, patient锯 sawtooth that rose and fell each year but never stopped rising overall. He had told his mother he understood it already. That was not quite true, though he liked to think of himself as someone for whom such things came easily, and so he kept the pretending up even alone.

The workbook wanted him to explain, in his own words, how greenhouse gases trapped heat. He wrote a sentence, crossed it out, and wrote it again. Something about the gases letting sunlight through and then holding the warmth the ground gave back, like a blanket that only worked one direction. His grandfather came through with a watering can and looked over his shoulder without comment, and Eli felt the old man's reticent attention as a kind of pressure, the way his grandfather would stand at a fence and watch weather come in without ever saying what he thought about it.

Sam arrived on a bicycle at noon, dust on the spokes, and proposed they walk out to the rock quarry past the windbreak of cedars, because Sam could not sit still in a house that smelled of coffee grounds and old paper. Eli brought the workbook anyway, folded into his back pocket, which Sam noticed and mocked with a look but not out loud.

The quarry was a pale gash in the hillside, terraced and quiet, with a shallow green pool at the bottom that neither of them would have swum in. It was there, throwing pebbles at a ledge, that Sam said the thing they would argue about for an hour. His older sister worked at an environmental nonprofit, and Sam had absorbed from her the conviction that methane was the real problem, that if you wanted to slow warming in the next few years you went after methane leaks from wells and pipelines and forgot about carbon dioxide for a while.

Eli, who had a presentiment that this was too simple, and who also simply enjoyed disagreeing with Sam, took the other side. He said the graph in his pocket was carbon dioxide, that the line had been climbing since before either of them was born, that carbon dioxide was the thing that stayed. He did not know at first what stayed meant, only that he had read it somewhere and it felt load-bearing.

Sam threw another pebble and then, unexpectedly, made the argument precise. He knew the numbers, or some of them. Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, he said, so molecule for molecule it mattered much more right now. Eli said that couldn't be the whole story or everyone would talk about methane all the time, and Sam said the catch was time. A methane molecule stays in the atmosphere only about a decade on average, much less time than carbon dioxide, which essentially hangs around for centuries. So methane hit harder and faded; carbon dioxide hit softer and accumulated.

Eli took the workbook out of his pocket and flattened it on a flat slab of quarry stone, and they bent over the rising line together. He tried to dichotomize the problem, the way Ms. Nwosu was always warning them against: fast gas versus slow gas, decade versus century. But the graph refused the split. The line kept its rhythm either way, a long debt that methane rules could not cancel, while a decade of stopped leaks, Sam insisted, would still buy real years. They could not make the two framings agree, and eventually they stopped trying and sat on the slab with their shoes off, feet hot on the stone, watching the pool below turn darker as a cloud crossed.

Later, walking back through the cedars, Eli admitted he had gotten the half-life wrong at first, or maybe he hadn't, or maybe the argument had gone differently than he remembered it, because he had been retelling it to himself all afternoon and each retelling smoothed a different edge. At the house his grandfather was watering the tomatoes again, water he had already given them that morning, and Eli stood at the fence beside him with the workbook still under his arm and watched the light go long and low across the field.

"Did you figure it out?" his grandfather asked, and Eli said, "Some of it," which was the most accurate sentence he'd produced all day.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Affirming the consequent is a logical fallacy: from 'if P then Q' and 'Q', concluding 'P'. Living in San Diego means living in California, but living in California does not mean living in San Diego.
story:
Amy arrived at the coffee shop first, claiming the table by the window with her notebook open to a page that said, in her own handwriting, "Know this cold by Saturday." Saturday was the debate tournament, and the resolution was about school funding, and her opening argument, according to Samuel, had a hole in it large enough to drive a bus through. She was still deciding whether he was right.

Samuel dropped his bag on the chair across from her and slid his drink, some bombastic frozen thing with whipped cream and caramel, onto the table. "So say it again," he said. "The whole chain."

"Fine. If a school has a strong arts program, its students score higher on tests. Therefore, if students score higher on tests, the school must have a strong arts program."

Harper arrived mid-sentence, pulling out the third chair. "Must have?" she said. "That's the part I don't like. That's a big must."

"It's evidence," Amy said. "High scores are evidence of the arts program."

"Evidence isn't proof," Harper said, and blew on her tea.

Mr. Russo came over to wipe the table beside theirs, and Amy caught him half-smiling at her notebook. "Debate kids," he said. "You argue like my sister and me at dinner. She told me once, if it rained, the lawn is wet. Our lawn was wet, so it rained. And I said, Ann, I ran the sprinkler this morning."

Amy put her pen down. Something shifted in her head, the way a puzzle piece turns before it clicks. "Wait," she said. "The lawn being wet doesn't mean it rained, because the sprinkler also makes the lawn wet."

"Affirming the consequent," Samuel said, sounding pleased with himself. "It's called affirming the consequent."

"Say the whole thing," Harper said, "because I want to see if I actually follow it."

Samuel drew in the condensation on his cup. "If P then Q. If it rained, the lawn is wet. Now take Q, the lawn is wet, and conclude P, so it rained. That's the fallacy. The wet lawn follows from rain, but rain isn't the only thing that makes a lawn wet."

Amy wrote it out under the resolution and looked at it a long moment. "So the one-way thing is the problem. Like San Diego and California. If you live in San Diego, you live in California. But if you live in California, you don't have to live in San Diego. You could live anywhere in the state. The arrow only goes one direction."

"And high test scores," Harper said slowly, "could come from a lot of places. Tutoring. Wealth. A stratum of families who can afford test prep. You can't run the arrow backwards and say the arts program must be there."

Amy felt the strange double weight of it: relief at finding the flaw, and annoyance that the flaw was in her own case. She had built the argument over two evenings, and now she could see the seam where she had welded evidence into certainty. "So I can still say the arts program is sufficient for higher scores," she tried. "I just can't say it's necessary. If arts, then higher scores, maybe. Higher scores, then arts, no."

"Maybe you say it as a conditional and hold the line there," Harper said. "If the program exists and scores rise, that's consistent with your claim. It doesn't prove it alone, but it's consistent."

"Consistent," Amy repeated, and wrote that word down too, and underlined it twice. She was starting to think the whole tournament might be about which team noticed which direction their arrows pointed. "But here's what I still don't know," she said. "If I can't run the arrow backwards, how does anyone ever prove anything? Wet lawns, high scores, all of it just stays consistent forever?"

Samuel shrugged. "Maybe you collect enough other causes and rule them out. Maybe you never fully get there."

"That's terrifying," Amy said.

"That's Saturday," Harper said.

Mr. Russo came back with a cloth and a refill of water nobody had asked for, and set it in the middle of the table like an offering. "My sister never conceded a dinner argument in her life," he said. "You three are more honest than she is." He laughed and went back behind the counter.

Amy looked at her page, at the neat little chain she had written and the crooked line she had drawn through its conclusion. She could codify the fix as a rule, write if-then in the left margin and never cross the arrow again, and probably she would. But she left the crossed-out sentence visible rather than erasing it, because she wanted to be able to see where she had gone wrong, in case she went wrong there again. On the top of a fresh page she wrote, "Sufficient is not necessary," and beneath it, in smaller letters, "What am I still missing?"

"Okay," she said, capping her pen and pulling the resolution toward her. "Samuel, you're the other team. Come at me. Sprinklers and all."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In a 2011 Stanford study, basketball players who aimed for 10 hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10.
story:
Alexander spread his notebook across the bench outside the gym, smoothing the page where he had ruled columns for Monday through Sunday. The plan was due to Ms. Wilson by the end of the week, and he had promised her something ambitious: a full training program for basketball, complete with rest days and warm-ups, the kind of thing a real athlete might follow. So far the page held drills, sprints, shooting practice on Tuesday and Thursday, and a blank space where Sunday ought to be. Sunday resisted him. He could not decide whether rest was a weakness or a strategy.

Derrick dropped onto the bench beside him with his phone already out. "Let me see." He turned the notebook toward the light. "You've got practice every single day except Sunday, and even then you wrote a question mark."

"That's the part I can't figure out," Alexander said. "Whether the question mark is the point."

Derrick laughed. "You ascribe too much meaning to empty boxes." He tapped the Sunday column with one finger. "Rest is just nothing. It's the absence of a plan."

Audrey-Anne arrived from the library with a folder of printouts under her arm, and she sat on the bench's far end, arranging her papers as though setting a small table. "Ms. Wilson gave me the same assignment," she said. "I found a study you should look at before you fill that in."

Alexander leaned over. The printout showed a table of numbers, and at the top, a line about Stanford, 2011, and basketball players. "What am I looking at?"

"Sleep," Audrey-Anne said. "The players in the study aimed for ten hours in bed every night. Not training, just being in bed. And their free throws went from 7.9 out of ten to 8.8 out of ten over the study."

Derrick squinted at the page. "That's almost one more make per ten shots. From lying in bed."

"That's what the numbers say," Audrey-Anne said. "I didn't run it. They did."

Alexander copied the figures into his notebook, 7.9 and 8.8, and sat back. Inside the gym, through the propped door, he could hear the JV squad running lines, shoes squeaking in a rhythm that rose and fell like something breathing. He watched them, and he thought about his own week, the way he had stacked drills into every evening and then stayed up past two most nights, shooting on the driveway until the porch light clicked off, telling himself the extra hours were the difference between him and everyone else.

His phone buzzed. It was a message from his older brother, who played at a college two states away and rarely wrote anything longer than a sentence.

Saw your plan on the fridge when I was home. Looks good. One thing. I used to plan every drill and still stay up till 2. Coaches finally sat me down. Sleep is training too. Quit treating rest like it's cheating.

Alexander read it twice, then held the screen out so Derrick and Audrey-Anne could see. "He says rest is training."

Derrick read it and made a face like he'd bitten into something sour. "That sounds like something a tired person says to feel better about napping."

"It sounds like something a person with a shooting percentage says," Audrey-Anne said mildly. She tapped her printout. "You can be pugnacious about the weights room all you want, but the numbers in this study didn't come from arguing."

"I'm not being pugnacious," Derrick said, though the set of his shoulders suggested otherwise. "I'm saying one study doesn't settle it. What if those players were just bad free-throw shooters to start with? 7.9 isn't great."

"It went to 8.8," Alexander said. "The direction is the part that matters to me." He looked at his notebook again, at the question mark sitting in Sunday's box, and at the columns for Tuesday and Thursday, which now seemed crowded. He uncapped his pen, crossed out Thursday's second drill, and wrote, in small letters, in bed by 10:30. Then, under Sunday, he wrote rest, deliberately, with no question mark.

"That's it?" Derrick said. "You're going to hand Ms. Wilson a plan where the hardest part is a bedtime?"

"The hardest part of my plan is whatever I was doing before," Alexander said. "Drills until midnight and then wondering why Thursday's shots wouldn't fall." He thought about saying more, some tidy sentence about what he had decided, but the truth was less tidy. He did not know whether ten hours in bed would work for him the way it had worked for the players in the study, or whether his Tuesday routine was already right and he was only rearranging it to feel virtuous. He knew only that he had been treating exhaustion as proof of effort, and the numbers on Audrey-Anne's printout had quietly called that chicanery, a trick he had been running on himself.

Ms. Wilson came out of the gym with a clipboard under her arm and a whistle hanging against her collar. She paused by the bench. "Plans coming along?"

"Alexander has a bedtime in his," Derrick said, grinning.

Ms. Wilson looked at the notebook, at the crossed-out drill, at the Sunday column, and said nothing for a long moment. Then she picked up the pen, turned to Monday's warm-up box, and wrote something small at the bottom before handing the notebook back. Alexander looked. She had written, get sleep the night before, and underlined it once.

He closed the notebook, slid it into his bag with the printout folded inside, and stood. Through the gym door the JV squad had stopped running lines and were at the far basket, shooting free throws, one after another, the ball snapping off the rim and then, for one of them, dropping clean through.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Circumlocution, describing a word you cannot remember instead of stopping, is a recognized communication strategy that keeps a second-language speaker talking.
story:
Wyatt set his phone on the kitchen table, screen up, timer ready, and his grandfather's dog immediately put one paw on it as if to vote against the whole enterprise. "Off," Wyatt said, and the dog, whose name was Biscuit and who understood no French whatsoever, wagged.

The assignment was simple and terrible: five minutes, entirely in French, arguing whether the city should make public transit free, and it was due Thursday. It was Tuesday. He had exactly one advantage, which was that he was spending these two days at his grandparents' house, and his grandfather had grown up in Lyon and still muttered at crossword puzzles in two languages.

"Papi," Wyatt said, switching over, "can I argue at you for a bit?"

His grandfather looked up from the newspaper, peevish about being interrupted mid-sudoku but too polite to say so. "Argue away. But I charge a fee. One slice of toast."

"Deal. Start the timer." Wyatt hit the phone with his knuckle and began. Public transit should be free because, because, because the money, the money the city collects from, from the thing you pay to the government, the thing that comes out of your paycheck, and his brain went entirely white. He stopped. Biscuit barked at nothing.

"Forty seconds," his grandfather said, chewing toast.

Wyatt dropped his forehead onto the table. "I forgot the word for tax. I can't debate without the word for tax. That's like half the debate."

His grandfather returned to his newspaper, and Wyatt, sulking productively, watched him read. After a while his grandfather tapped the crossword and said, in English, "Three across. The, ah, the instrument with keys, for the wind, you blow it and it is long, black, in an orchestra it sits, the clarinet's sad cousin." He wrote in the answer with no shame at all, as if talking around a word were simply how you got to the next word.

Wyatt sat up so fast the dog growled. "Wait. You do that. You forget words and you just describe them and keep going."

His grandfather shrugged. "Everyone does. In any language."

Wyatt grabbed his phone and texted Pierre, who was in his class and annoyingly good at French, and Pierre called him within a minute, Erik apparently already on the line because they did everything in a pile now. "I saw your text," Pierre said. "Yeah, it has a name. Circumlocution. Ms. Grant mentioned it like once and moved on."

"You're making it up."

"I'm making up nothing. Circumlocution. It's a real thing, it keeps you talking instead of stopping. Try it."

Erik's voice cut in from somewhere far away, probably his bedroom. "Do the tax thing. Say the money that the government takes, the money from work, the thing that eats your paycheck. Tax is four letters, Wyatt. You can carry a sentence around four letters."

The timer restarted. Wyatt went again, and when the white space opened where the word should be, he walked around it: the money that the government collects, the money that comes from salaries, the money that could, if the city wished, pay for buses instead. His grandfather raised his toast in salute. It was not graceful. It was a kind of verbal scaffolding, wobbling but standing, and at some point Wyatt noticed he had stopped translating in his head and started just talking, badly, fluently, the way you might describe a fire exit route to someone while the building was already smoky.

At the four-minute mark he ran out of arguments for free transit and had to argue against himself for the last minute, which his grandfather applauded at the end, one clap, like a man at a very small tennis match. "You monetize the buses, you don't give them away," Wyatt improvised, and then stopped, because he'd used the wrong verb and possibly invented a French word for it, and Erik's laughter came through the phone like a burst pipe.

"That's the spirit of the zeitgeist, though," Pierre said. "Everything monetized. That's your rebuttal section, you're welcome."

"One more time," Wyatt said, reaching for the timer. "Biscuit, this time you be the judge."

His grandfather folded the crossword, pushed the butter toward the middle of the table, and said, "Same fee."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Chicago style offers two citation systems: notes and bibliography, common in history and the humanities, and author-date, common in the sciences.
story:
Katherine spread the returned paper across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the pages with a jar of apricot preserves and a saucer with a hairline crack through its painted wren. Mr. Thompson had written a single line at the top in green ink, the kind teachers use when they are more tired than angry: "This is author-date. We use the other one." The margin of every page carried small corrections like insect tracks, arrows pointing footnote numbers down to the bottom of the page where no notes waited. The kitchen smelled of coffee gone cold and the lavender her grandmother kept in a bowl by the window, and outside a sprinkler ticked its slow circle across a lawn already wet.

She had written the paper on the Rhondda valleys, on why the miners' strikes of her great-grandfather's era had succeeded or failed depending on which historian she believed, and Mr. Thompson had circled her thesis and written "arguable, good" beside it, which had felt, for one afternoon, like sunlight. Then he had circled everything below it. On the last page her bibliography sat in parentheses, tidy and wrong: (Smith 1998, 44), (Griffiths 2003, 112), like a series of small confessions. She had chosen that form because it looked scientific, because it looked certain.

The house was quiet except for the sprinkler and her grandfather's radio murmuring cricket commentary from the next room. Katherine opened her laptop and typed the words from the green ink into the search bar. The results page filled with headings, and she sat back. Chicago style offered two citation systems, one page said, notes and bibliography, common in history and the humanities, and the other, author-date, common in the sciences. She read it twice. She had known about Chicago style, had chosen it deliberately over MLA because it seemed more serious, and had somehow never learned that it came in two kinds, like a road that forks so early you don't notice you've taken a branch.

She called Nika, who answered on the second ring with the sound of a bus behind her. "Did Thompson hand yours back?"

"Mine's fine," Nika said. "I did footnotes. Little numbers, sources at the bottom of the page. Montana did what you did, though, the parentheses. He got the same note."

"Why didn't he tell me he'd gotten it?"

"Because he's Montana. He said the whole thing catalyzed his distrust of formatting in general."

Katherine laughed, then stopped laughing, because something was bothering her. "Nika, why do history and the humanities use the notes? Why wouldn't everyone just use the same one?"

"Maybe because," Nika said, and then the bus noise swallowed her voice, and Katherine was left holding the question herself. It was a fair question, the kind Mr. Thompson liked. She looked at her grandfather's bookshelf, the shelf of mining histories she had worked from, and pulled one down. At the bottom of each page sat the little numbers and their small paragraphs of source, and it occurred to her that in a history paper the sources were partly the argument, the way a lawyer shows the jury not just a conclusion but the whole chain of testimony. In the sciences, from what she could see on her screen, the parentheses pointed outward, to data, to names and years, to things that could be checked fast. Two ways of trusting a reader. She wasn't sure that was right, and she wrote in her notebook, "Ask Thompson: is it about speed or about argument?" and underlined it, and then wrote, "or neither?"

She spent the afternoon converting. Her grandmother brought her toast with the preserves whose jar had been promoted from paperweight to lunch, and stood reading over her shoulder for a while. "That looks like your grandfather's sermons," her grandmother said. "All those little numbers. Like a detective's notebook." It was as close to the truth as anything Katherine had read that day.

By evening she had a draft of the new version, footnotes marching along the bottoms of pages, a bibliography that no longer spoke in parentheses, and a paragraph she had added near the end, one she had not planned. In it she admitted that the question of why the two systems existed had opened a larger one for her, whether the form of a paper could shape what it was able to say, whether writing history in the style of the sciences might quietly push a person toward conclusions that behaved more like facts than they should. She thought of her own parenthetical bibliography, how confident it had looked, how much culpability for that false confidence belonged to her own wish to seem certain, and how much was almost congenital to the format itself, something she had been born into as a writer without choosing. She left the paragraph in. She did not know if it belonged there.

She read the new version aloud once, quietly, testing the rhythm of the footnotes against her sentences, and then she emailed it to Mr. Thompson with a note: "Fixed the system, I think. Also added a question on page six that I couldn't answer. Is that allowed?"

She closed the laptop. The sprinkler had gone off somewhere in the dusk, and her grandfather's radio was playing the shipping forecast now, naming sea areas she would never see, and her grandmother was at the sink saying, "There's more jam if you want it."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Holding static stretches for a long time, about 60 seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive activity can briefly reduce strength and power, so many programs warm up with dynamic movement.
story:
Emile had until Monday to hand in the training program, and by Thursday night he still had nothing but a blank grid and his father's old maxim, taped to the fridge: no pain, no gain. Ms. Tehrani had assigned it to the whole sports science class, five days of sessions, two rest days, a warm-up protocol, all of it justified. He was supposed to be planning it for himself, a hockey player, and he knew what his father's version looked like: skate until the legs quit, every day, twice on Sundays.

He spread the grid on the kitchen table and started filling boxes. Monday, full ice. Tuesday, full ice. Wednesday, sprints at the track because the rink was booked. He was reaching for Thursday when Ada kicked the door open with her skate bag over one shoulder.

"You're doing the program too?" she said, dropping into the other chair. "Celine already finished hers. She's eulogizing it in the group chat like it's dead and buried and perfect." Ada leaned over his grid. "You've got no rest days."

"Rest is for the hedonistic," Emile said, and Ada laughed, which made him feel the grid was defended. But she pulled out her phone and showed him her own version: hard day, easy day, one day of nothing at all. "Ms. Tehrani says the adaptation happens on the rest days. Something gets rebuilt." He copied the shape of it, unsure. He had a vague sense that resting was lazy, and a vaguer sense that the sense was wrong.

The real problem surfaced Saturday morning at the community rink, where Emile had arranged to time Celine, who ran track in the fall and skated in the winter and was preparing for a fitness test on Tuesday. He got there early to lay out cones. Celine arrived, dropped her bag, and did what she always did before hard efforts: she sat on the blue line and held long, deep stretches, one muscle at a time, a full minute or more, breathing slow, eyes closed, methodical as prayer.

From Celine's side of the glass, the plan was simple. Emile would time her sprint laps, she'd log the numbers, and Monday's program would include whatever warm-up the stopwatch approved. She counted her stretches out of habit. Fifty-eight, fifty-nine, sixty. She switched legs. Emile was watching from the boards, and something about the counting bothered him, though he couldn't have said why yet. She stood, shook out her thighs, and told him she was ready.

The times were slow. Not dramatically, but enough: three-tenths on the first lap, worse on the second, and by the fourth her legs felt like they belonged to somebody tired. "I'm flat," she said, hands on her knees. "I'm always flat in races. Everyone says I choke on the start line." Emile didn't answer, because a memory had surfaced. At the track in September, a sprinter from another school had sat on the start line holding a long stretch, sixty seconds at least, and had come out of the blocks like a different, slower person. Emile had noticed and filed it away as nothing.

"Stop stretching," he said. "Just move. Skips, leg swings, things in motion." Celine looked at him as if he'd told her to skip brushing her teeth. But the test was Tuesday and the times were bad, so she tried it. Arm circles, walking lunges, high knees along the boards, everything swinging and brief, nothing held. Then they ran the laps again. Her first effort was faster than anything from the earlier set, and her legs, she kept saying, felt springy, which was not a word either of them used lightly.

They sat on the bench afterward with the phone between them, comparing numbers. "Holding static stretches for a long time, sixty seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive stuff can briefly reduce your strength and power," Emile said slowly, reading off his own notes, testing the sentence against what they'd watched happen. "So programs warm up with dynamic movement instead." It fit. It fit the sprinter in September, and it fit Celine's whole fall season of feeling flat after her start-line ritual, which nobody had ever connected to the ritual itself.

What he couldn't settle, walking home with the grid folded in his jacket pocket, was whether the stretches were still good for her on other days, away from the racing, and where exactly the line fell between a stretch that helped and one that stole her legs. He wrote the dynamic warm-up into Monday's plan anyway, Monday now a hard day and Tuesday now rest, his father's maxim retired to the fridge. Celine texted him a photo of her splits from the second set, then a second message: "So do I stretch on Wednesday or not?" He looked at the question for a long time and typed, "I'll find out."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In common-law countries such as the US, UK and Canada, a contract generally needs an offer, an acceptance and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange.
story:
The phone store smelled of floor polish and warm plastic, and Henry had been standing at the counter for eleven minutes while the manager typed his mother's details into a form that seemed to grow longer the more he answered it. His old phone had died on Tuesday, two days before the regional debate tournament, and without a working device he could not receive the schedule changes his coach sent out at midnight, a habit the whole team had learned to dread and rely on.

"You need a parent present, or a signed authorization," the manager said. "She has to initial here, here, and here. It's the terms and conditions. Everybody under eighteen gets the same treatment."

"My mom's at work until nine," Henry said. "The tournament starts tomorrow at eight. The first round pairings come out tonight."

The manager looked almost sorry, which was somehow worse than blase indifference would have been. He slid a printed contract across the counter, dense with clauses about liability and cancellation fees, and Henry read it the way he read debate evidence, hunting for the thing that would either save him or sink him.

That was where Janice found him, still reading, twenty minutes later. She had come in to buy a screen protector and was carrying her binder of chemistry notes under one arm like a briefcase.

"Are you seriously reading the whole thing?" she said.

"I'm looking for a loophole. There has to be one. This is like twelve pages."

"Nobody reads those. You just scroll to the bottom and tap agree."

"That's the part that bothers me," Henry said. "You consent to something you've never actually seen. My debate coach would call that being disenfranchised from your own decisions, except he only uses that word about voting." He tapped a paragraph near the top. "Look, it says the company isn't liable for water damage. But it also says they'll replace a water-damaged phone once per year. Both things can't be true, can they?"

Janice leaned over the counter, and while she read, Henry told her about the tutoring deal he'd made with Natalya the week before. He would coach her in public speaking for the tournament, and she had promised to pay him forty dollars from her birthday money, in writing, on a napkin from the cafeteria, complete with both their signatures.

"So is that a real contract?" Janice asked. "A napkin?"

"I asked Mr. Byrne about it this morning, before homeroom. He teaches business law in the fall, so I figured he'd know." Henry had caught him in the hallway, coffee in hand, and Mr. Byrne had said only one thing before the bell, something Henry had been turning over ever since. What Mr. Byrne said is that in common-law countries such as the US, UK and Canada, a contract generally needs an offer, an acceptance, and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange.

"Consideration," Janice repeated. "So her forty dollars is her side of it."

"And my tutoring is mine," Henry said. "So the napkin might actually count." He looked down at the twelve pages under his hands, and something rearranged itself in his head, the way two debate cases clicked together when you found the shared assumption underneath them. "Which means this thing is the same animal, just bigger. They offer me a phone, I accept by signing, and I give them money every month. It's all the same three pieces, whether it's written on a napkin or printed on twelve pages by a company with lawyers."

The manager returned with a laminated card about activation fees. Henry asked him whether the water-damage clause and the replacement promise contradicted each other, and the manager admitted, after a pause, that the replacement program was a separate document Henry would have to sign as well, with its own terms. A separate offer, Henry thought. A separate acceptance. The stack of things he was agreeing to kept revealing layers, like water found deeper and deeper in the same aquifer, and he began to wonder how far down it went, and whether anyone had ever reached the bottom.

At four o'clock his phoneless watch showed forty minutes until the store closed, and he still had no plan. He tried calling his mother from the store's display phone, but she didn't pick up, and the manager had begun straightening the accessory wall in the deliberate way of someone marking time.

Then Natalya walked in. She had come to buy a charger, and when she heard about the deadline she pulled out her own phone and called Henry's mother directly, because she sold raffle tickets to her every autumn and knew her voice. Henry listened to Natalya explain the situation, calm and structured, using the exact phrasing he had drilled into her for their practice rounds, and he thought about the napkin in his pocket, and the forty dollars, and whether teaching someone to speak could be counted as something of value or whether it only felt that way to him.

His mother's voice came through the speaker, tinny and tired. "Read me the parts I have to sign," she said. "All of them. I'm not initialing anything I haven't heard."

Henry picked up the contract, found the first clause, and started reading aloud while Natalya listened and Janice held the page flat against the counter. "Section four," he began. "Liability and limitation."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Higher interest rates pay savers more, so households tend to shift some money from spending into savings, which lowers demand for goods and helps slow price rises.
story:
The bank smelled of carpet cleaner and cold air, and the savings rate on the wall display had changed since June. Ryder stood at the counter with his summer paycheck warm in his back pocket and read the number twice. Up. Almost a full point higher than when he'd opened the account in May.

He had the phone picked out already. Max had sent him the link a week ago, a message that read, "This is the one. Camera's unreal. Stop being cheap." Ryder had screenshotted it and kept it on his phone like a promise he'd made to someone else.

"Deposit or withdrawal?" the teller asked.

He hesitated long enough that the man behind him shifted his weight. "Deposit," Ryder said. "All of it."

Outside, he sat on the concrete planter and texted Max: putting it in savings instead. The reply came fast, a string of question marks, then: "you've had that phone since sophomore year. it dies at 40%." Ryder typed and deleted three answers before settling on the truth, or part of it: "the rate went up. they're paying more now." Max sent back a single word, "bombastic," which was Max's way of saying he thought Ryder was being dramatic, and then: "they pay you like nine dollars a year."

That stung because it was true. He did the math on his thumb against the planter's edge. His paycheck, the new rate, the months until spring. It was not a fortune. It was, in fact, barely a case for the phone. But he kept circling something Mr. Novák had said at the end of econ before school let out, not a lecture, just a line tossed over his shoulder as he erased the board: "Watch the bank rates this summer, if you want to see the whole economy breathing." Ryder had written it down because Mr. Novák never said anything twice.

He walked to the library and pulled up the central bank's statement from his phone's browser, the smell of the bank still in his nose, that clean chemical cold. The language was dense. He read a paragraph three times, then tried to parametrize it in his own head, reducing it to a few variables he could actually hold: rates go up, banks pay savers more. That part he had lived, standing at the counter. Then the second part, the one that hadn't clicked until he was walking: when people get paid more to save, some of them move money out of spending and into savings. Him, literally him, an hour ago. If enough households did that, there was less money chasing goods, less demand, and prices stopped climbing so fast. That was the chain. Inflation slowing wasn't a button someone pressed. It was a million people standing at counters making his exact decision, phone-less, patient.

But there was a piece he couldn't close. He'd wanted that phone since March. Saving instead felt less like strategy and more like deprivation with a theory attached, and he couldn't fully tell the difference. Maybe the smart move was both, half in savings, half toward the phone. Maybe that was what most people did, and maybe that was why inflation never died cleanly, because everyone hedged a little. He texted Azaan, who was working at his uncle's shop until September: "if the bank pays you more to save, and you save instead of buying stuff, demand drops and prices cool. yes or no." Azaan, who trusted no summary he hadn't checked, replied twenty minutes later: "checked w my uncle. basically. he calls it everyone tightening at once." Then: "also are you still buying the phone or what."

Ryder looked at his reflection in the dark library window, the old phone in his hand with its hairline crack across the corner, its battery gauge that had learned to lie. There was a remittance slip folded in his wallet from money he'd mailed his grandmother in the spring, back when the rate had been nothing and saving had seemed pointless, and he took it out now and smoothed it flat on the table. Two different springs, two different logics. He had sent that money because family came first no matter what the rate said, and he was saving this money partly because the rate said to, and both of those were true of the same person, and he could not make them into one clean principle no matter how he arranged it.

He typed to both of them at once: "half in savings, half for the phone. meet me friday."

Max answered first: "finally."

Azaan answered second: "so the economy breathes anyway."

Ryder slid the old phone into his pocket, feeling its cracked edge catch on the seam.
